Matthew Flatt, Shriram Krishnamurthi, and Matthias Felleisen. Classes and mixins. In Proc.
    25th ACM SIGPLAN-SIGACT Symposium on Principles of Programming Languages,
    POPL ’98, pp. 171–183. Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA,
    1998. doi:10.1145/268946.268961. This paper is one of the earliest works using mixin
    inheritance after those of Bracha himself, and shows how Java, a familiar language (to
    the masses) could be extended to support mixin inheritance. The authors define a dialect
    of Java with mixin inheritance, MixedJava, to illustrate the approach taken in MzScheme.
    MixedJava is based on ClassicJava, a simplified model of Java. Like Java, ClassicJava
    has single inheritance. Mixins are defined as second-class functions that take a super-
    class as parameter and extend it to a new class combined with the mixin. New classes
    can then be declared by combining mixins. The semantics of those mixins is more con-
    vincingly described in the 2006 sequel, in which attempt of doing things with Java and
    its types is dropped, and simpler first-class classes and mixins are used instead. I admit
    I like the idea, but the choice of Java makes me less interested, with all the time spent
    describing Java-like semantics being a waste of time. I also admit I suspect the authors
    share my taste, but chose Java precisely because much of the intended public has opposite
    preferences.
Brian Foote and Joseph W. Yoder. Big Ball of Mud. In Proc. PLoP, 1997. http://www.
    laputan.org/mud/ A very entertaining yet also enlightening essay about the good and
    bad things that often happen as developers build software in the large. The authors give
    names to common phenomena they describe, borrowing metaphors from architecture and
    urban development. A great read for who wants to think about software at a scale larger
    than code.
Nate Foster, M. Greenwald, J. T. Moore, B. Pierce, and A. Schmitt. Combinators for bidi-
    rectional tree transformations: A linguistic approach to the view-update problem. ACM
    Trans. Program. Lang. Syst. 29, 2007. doi:10.1145/1232420.1232424. Extended ver-
    sion of the seminal POPL 2005 paper. A very formal treatment of lenses, yet with con-
    crete applications on how to edit a view on some data structure and reflect the changes
    back onto an updated value for the data structure. I admit too formal for my tastes.
Michael L. Fredman, János Komlós, and Endre Szemerédi. Storing a Sparse Table with
    O(1) Worst Case Access Time. Journal of the ACM 31(3), pp. 538–544, 1984.
    doi:10.1145/828.1884. The paper introduces the classic FKS perfect-hashing construc-
    tion (as it would later be called), which achieves what the title says: compact constant-
    time lookup structures for a static sparse table. The search for a perfect solution can take
    a lot of time, and the authors propose probabilistic search with a high probability of find-
    ing a good-enough solution in finite time. This kind of technique can be used to speed
    up field access in records with known shapes, and thus also method lookup and subtype
    tests.
Daniel P. Friedman, Christopher T. Haynes, and Mitchell Wand. Essentials of Program-
    ming Languages. 3rd edition. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, USA, 2008.
    doi:10.5555/1378240. EOPL is a great classic about Programming Languages. How-
    ever, its chapter on OO only has classes with single inheritance. EOPL barely touches
    multiple inheritance, “powerful, but . . . problematic”, in exercise 9.26, and prototypes in
    exercise 9.27-9.29. Disappointing on the OO front.
Daniel P. Friedman and Amr Sabry. Recursion is a Computational Effect. Computer Science
    Department, Indiana University, TR546, Bloomington, Indiana, USA, 2000. https:
    //homes.luddy.indiana.edu/sabry/files/recursion-monads-tr.pdf The
    authors compare unfolding and updating interpretations of fixed points, and observe that
ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY                                                                     363

    they are equivalent in pure calculi but behave differently in the presence of computational
    effects. They then study three variants of monadic fixed points in Haskell, and argue
    that recursion should itself be treated as a computational effect. A good reference for
    distinguishing pure, lazy and stateful operational realizations of recursion.
Richard P. Gabriel. Essays. 2002. https://www.dreamsongs.com/Essays.html Many
    great essays are listed on rpg’s webpage, but for the sake of criticizing OO, his OOSPLA
    2002 debate where he and Brian Foote took the position “Objects Have Failed” against
    Guy Steele and James Noble, is relevant to the critique of OO.
Richard P. Gabriel. The Structure of a Programming Language Revolution. In Proc. ACM
    international symposium on New ideas, new paradigms, and reflections on programming
    and software, pp. 195–214, 2012. doi:10.1145/2384592.2384611. A magnificent pa-
    per that discusses how different people think about software (and everything else) in
    often incommensurable paradigms. In the illustrative example, old timers and Lispers
    approach programming with a “system” paradigm, whereas the academic and industrial
    mainstream since sometime in the 1980s has a very different “language” paradigm. Inter-
    estingly, the paper it rightfully excoriates for its authors’ paradigmatic misunderstanding
    of OO due to their language paradigm, is also one of the best papers on the semantics of
    OO, the Bracha & Cook 1990. I suspect it was Cook who wrote the more paradigmat-
    ically foreign parts of the paper, for I personally know Bracha to very much follow the
    system paradigm (see his beautiful work on Newspeak). He still wrongly believes mixin
    inheritance to be more modular than multiple inheritance, though.
Richard P. Gabriel, Jon L White, and Daniel G. Bobrow. CLOS: Integrating Object-Oriented
    and Functional Programming. Communications of the ACM 34(9), pp. 29–38, 1991.
    doi:10.1145/114669.114671. An informal overview of CLOS and its many features.
Michael Gale. Hoop. 2015. https://github.com/mbg/hoop/ (accessed 2026-02-05).
    Originally published as MSH in 2015, then renamed to Hoop in 2020, Hoop is a pure
    functional object system written in Haskell, providing second-class classes with single
    inheritance. Hoop uses template Haskell to provide a nice syntax to the underlying func-
    tionality, where manually expanding said syntax would be verbose and redundant; but it
    does not “cheat” in any way, e.g. by using some unsafe magic, non-standard compiler
    extension, or non-local code transformations.
Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, and John Vlissides. Design patterns: elements
     of reusable object-oriented software. Addison-Wesley, 1994. https://hillside.n
     et/elements- of- reusable- object- oriented- software- book The classic
     and influential “Gang of Four” (GoF) book on Design Patterns. Much loved, much hated.
     The book collects wisdom from practitioners: practical solutions to recurring issues often
     found in actual OO software development, that developers of the time could immediately
     apply in the industrial OO languages of the day (C++ 2.0 and Smalltalk).
          The book doesn’t discuss how simple language improvements could solve issues,
     because most programmers then (and still now) didn’t have this ability; it does briefly
     cite other OO languages (CLOS, Self, Dylan, Eiffel) and their capabilities, but doesn’t
     dwell on them. I see no issue with the book itself, but instead with the following it had,
     from people taking the wrong lessons from it—elevating the book as canon and eternal
     theory. The authors are not scientists and don’t claim to be; they lack the proper concepts
     that would bring enlightenment (that even scientists were lacking at the time); and they
     do their best with folk explanations that do not constitute theory at all.
          Here is a good reason to love design patterns and those who identify them: Design
     patterns are good, very important, essential even, as necessary first steps—to notice and
364                                                        ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY

      identify the drudgery involved in coding software, so it can later be automated away and
      eliminated, should the patterns keep reoccurring. For the same reason, it is stupid to fawn
      at design patterns as if they are permanent solutions, and a normal thing to collect then
      keep using over and over in the long run; and it is proper to hate representations of design
      patterns as such. To quote Rich Hickey, «Patterns mean “I have run out of language.”»
      I.e. patterns are fourth class entities manually processed by humans; but it is always
      preferrable, and always possible, to instead have first-class or second-class that automate
      the problem away.
           Therefore, in a decent language, there is only One Design Pattern: Use, extend,
      evolve and maintain the language and its libraries of functions and macros. But that
      indeed requires macros, and most languages don’t have them. Lisp does. Most “blub”
      languages utterly lack macros, or have very limited macros; a few languages support
      “compile-time reflection” or “templates”, mechanisms that are several orders of magni-
      tude more complex than Lisp macros, lack modularity, and require a completely different
      language, set of libraries and/or mental programming model, compared to regular use of
      the language, making them further unavailable to regular programmers.
           Now, even in a decent language, automation can be expensive; moreover, learning
      how to operate automation incurs its own cognitive burden. And so sometimes indeed,
      it is preferrable not to automate the design pattern and leave it as such, at least for the
      time being. But only if the pattern is so simple or seldom used, or so subtle in its intricate
      dependencies, that the automation required to apply it correctly is more complex and
      costlier than you can afford given your own limited applications, even with AI lowering
      the costs. Being too poor to afford automation is a sad state of affairs—but often it does
      happen and then you’re glad you have patterns.
           What is very wrong indeed is being satisfied with just having identified a pattern,
      being unaware of the possibility and necessity of automation or being wilfully blind to it,
      accepting blub languages that make automation unaffordable, being unwilling to pay the
      cost of moving away from these soul-crushing languages, lacking a soul to be crushed by
      these languages to begin with, or neglecting and corrupting the soul you do have.
Jacques Garrigue. Code reuse through polymorphic variants. In Proc. Workshop on Founda-
    tions of Software Engineering, 13, 2000. https://www.math.nagoya-u.ac.jp/~g
    arrigue/papers/fose2000.html The paper demonstrates how polymorphic vari-
    ants in OCaml (extensible variant types with row polymorphism), enable code reuse in
    a modular, extensible way. Importantly, the author shows how and why extensions to
    type descriptors in general need not try to be anything like subtypes of the inherited type.
    Garrigue’s approach would provide a much saner and powerful foundation to OO than
    the existing object system, if only it could be combined with open recursion of modules.
    Unhappily, OCaml support for subtyping and recursive modules is limited, and so it is
    unclear whether a complete and better object system could be built this way on top of the
    current OCaml.
Jean-Yves Girard. Interprétation fonctionnelle et élimination des coupures de l’arithmétique
    d’ordre supérieur. PhD dissertation, Université Paris VII, 1972. https://girard.per
    so.math.cnrs.fr/These.pdf Girard’s famous thesis introduced what is now called
    System F, a second-order intuitionistic proof system whose computational counterpart
    Reynolds independently rediscovered in 1974 as a polymorphic typed 𝜆-calculus.
ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY                                                                     365

GitHub. The top programming languages. 2022. https://octoverse.github.com/2
    022/top-programming-languages (accessed 2024-01-04). Since that study was
    published, a lot of the JavaScript code has ceded first place to TypeScript; still basically
    the same language, same ecosystem, still supporting prototypes as well as classes, just
    with types. Ask your AI to find the latest update.
Joseph A. Goguen. Sheaf Semantics for Concurrent Interacting Objects. Mathematical Struc-
    tures in Computer Science 2(2), pp. 159–191, 1992. doi:10.1017/S0960129500001420.
    One of many papers by Goguen, who mixes the vocabulary of OO and the mathemat-
    ical approach of category theory to model the semantics of programs. In this paper he
    identifies “inheritance relations” with “sheaf morphisms”, which in layman terms means
    a refinement calculus wherein the “subclass” behavior cannot change anything to the
    superclass behavior, only add more details. This is completely different from what ev-
    eryone else calls OO, inheritance, etc. Now, refinement is an interesting concept, and
    AFAICT, Goguen contributes meaningful to its use. But the wilful and systematic abuse
    of words, stealing them from a then-trendy field, so as to ascribe them different concepts
    that already had perfectly good names, is, well, deceitful marketing at best.
Adele Goldberg and David Robson. Smalltalk-80: The Language and its Implementation.
    Addison-Wesley, Reading, Massachusetts, 1983. http://stephane.ducasse.free.
    fr/FreeBooks/BlueBook/Bluebook.pdf This seminal book (often called the “Blue
    Book”) provides the definitive description of the Smalltalk-80 language, including syn-
    tax, object model, classes and instances, metaclasses, protocols, and the standard library
    classes; even the compiler and interpreter and their optimizations.
         The language has single inheritance only. Each class has its own “metaclass” where
    metaclasses have an inheritance hierarchy parallel to classes, such that class-level pro-
    gramming is effectively a form of Prototype OO. Among many other things, the book
    introduces the terms abstract class and concrete class.
Ira P. Goldstein and Daniel G. Bobrow. Extending Object Oriented Programming in Smalltalk.
      In Proc. Proceedings of the 1980 ACM Conference on LISP and Functional Program-
      ming, LFP ’80, pp. 75–81. Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA,
      1980. doi:10.1145/800087.802792. This paper describes PIE, a knowledge representa-
      tion system implemented in Smalltalk-76. PIE combines frame-based ideas from KRL
      and FRL: each Node in its description network can acquire multiple Perspectives dynam-
      ically, each supplying specialized behavior and its own state. This constitutes a form of
      per-instance (flavorless) multiple inheritance, implemented as a layer on top of Smalltalk
      rather than as an extension to Smalltalk’s object system. This distinction is sharper in
      Smalltalk than in Lisp, where syntactic extensibility blurs the difference.
John B. Goodenough. Structured exception handling. In Proc. 2nd ACM SIGACT-
    SIGPLAN Symposium on Principles of Programming Languages, POPL ’75, pp.
    204–224. Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 1975.
    doi:10.1145/512976.512997. Goodenough proposes an approach to exception han-
    dling, and compares it to contemporary alternatives. He notably describes his colleague
    Douglas Ross’s 1967 “AED free storage package” as having “object-oriented exception
    handlers”.
        The description is a retrospective characterization by Goodenough in 1975: the origi-
    nal paper (written while Ross was at MIT) mentions “error” rather than “exceptions” and
    speaks of “zones” of storage allocation without calling their reified descriptors “objects”.
    What Goodenough seems to mean by the term is that when allocation from a zone fails,
    an “error procedure FERR” (original term by Ross) associated with the zone is called to
366                                                     ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY

      handle the error, as opposed to, e.g., lexically scoped error handlers as in Goodenough’s
      approach.
          In my terminology (roughly descended from Wegner 1987), the AED free storage
      package approach counts as “object-based”, but not “object-oriented”, since AED pro-
      vides no inheritance mechanism through which these object-associated handlers can be
      extended. However, Goodenough’s use of “object-oriented” shows that the term was “in
      the air” at the time.
Paul Graham. On Lisp: Advanced Techniques for Common Lisp. Prentice Hall, 1994. https:
     //paulgraham.com/onlisptext.html A book on practical software development
     in Lisp, with much focus on how to define and use macros. The section on anaphoric
     macros generated a fad among Common Lispers, happily short-lived after they realized
     the benefits are not worth the costs. Chapter 20 may have inspired several CPS transform
     libraries for Lisp. Chapter 25 is an alright introduction to OO, but mixes in one chapter
     what his 1995 book does better in two separate chapters: teaching CLOS, and explaining
     OO in general. Graham’s style is abductive: he has absorbed the concepts, but tries to
     lead the reader to it via a hands on approach, rather than explaining the theory.
Paul Graham. ANSI Common Lisp. Prentice Hall Series in Artificial Intelligence. Prentice
    Hall, Englewood Cliffs, NJ, 1995. https://archive.org/details/ansicommon
    lisp00grah A good introduction to Common Lisp. Chapter 10 is a solid introduction
    to CLOS. Chapter 17 is an impressive walk through to implement your own increasingly
    elaborate object system. As usual, Graham has a great style for a tutorial, taking you to
    the place you need to be, building understanding incrementally through examples rather
    than abstract theory, in an elegant and practical style.
Paul Graham. Beating the Averages. 2001a. https://paulgraham.com/avg.html
    (accessed 2026-01-19). A classic essay on how the expressiveness of Lisp helped Paul
    Graham and his associates implement and copy features faster than competition, which
    was key to the success of their business.
Paul Graham. Why Arc Isn’t Especially Object-Oriented. 2001b. https://paulgraham.c
     om/noop.html (accessed 2026-02-07). A short but interesting essay on why OO may be
     (or have been) overhyped and overused, with an interesting reply by Jonathan Rees about
     what OO may or may not be to begin with.
Radu Grigore. Java Generics are Turing Complete. In Proc. 44th ACM SIGPLAN Symposium
    on Principles of Programming Languages (POPL), POPL ’17, pp. 73–85. ACM, 2017.
    doi:10.1145/3009837.3009871. Grigore builds Turing machines inside the Java type-
    checking language, with O(n2 ) code the size of the Turing machine. Oops. So much for
    sacrificing power in exchange for guarantees: you have no guarantees, and no power for
    good but still all the power for evil.
Robin Hanson. The Age of Em: Work, Love, and Life when Robots Rule the Earth. Oxford
    University Press, Oxford, 2016. https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780198754
    626.001.0001 Hanson imagines what how societies of emulated beings with silicon
    substrate, that could react up to a million times faster than humans, would organize and
    interact with the comparatively slow humans. He anticipates that these beings would start
    as emulated human brains (hence Em) rather than as synthetic AIs, but this hypothesis
    is only important for a small part of the discussion. More interesting aspects are the
    societies being made of nested “forks” of some initial being, some long term, some short
    term. Also the cost of speed, versus the cost of duration, the impedance mismatch when
    communicating with beings running at different speeds, etc.

Timothy P. Hart. MACRO Definitions for LISP. MIT Artificial Intelligence Project, AI Memo,
    57, 1963. https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/6111 The first paper on
    Lisp macros. Note how LISP 1.5 was very primitive at the time: S-expressions had
    been the primary notation for actual code among Lispers since Steve Russell first hand-
    coded an implementation of EVAL in 1958; but M-expressions were still used for the
    theory; and toplevel definitions had a special syntax separate from expression syntax.
    M-expressions would fall into complete disuse as interactive Lisp made S-expressions
    a self-sufficient surface syntax through the REPL: once programmers could read, write,
    evaluate and define everything directly as S-expressions, the never-fully-formalized M-
    expression notation could only introduce discrepancies.
         The REPL concept was introduced by L. Peter Deutsch on the first Lisp interpreter
    with a “READ-EVAL-PRINT cycle”, his 1963 PDP-1 LISP, documented in 1964. Moon
    called it “read-eval-print loop” in the Maclisp manual in 1974. Schemers acronymized it
    as REPL in the 1980s. Greenblatt’s PDP-6 LISP in 1966 used only S-expressions, having
    made toplevel definitions uniform with expression syntax by replacing EVALQUOTE by
    EVAL for the REPL. But he introduced the more recognizable DEFUN syntax only as
    PDP-6 LISP evolved into MACLISP in 1969.
         The memo also has a variety of bugs, some more obvious (see acarrico’s transcript
    on GitHub), some more subtle (see Steele 1993), that you may find interesting to hunt.
Bob Hathaway. comp.object FAQ. 1996. http://www.faqs.org/faqs/object-faq/
    (accessed 2026-09-25). An extensive contemporary FAQ on object-oriented technology,
    representing common lore from 1993 to 1996. What I grew up believing OO to be, and
    what made me despise it for its hodgepodge complexity, reminding me of the quip at-
    tributed to Whitehead: “taxonomy is the death of science”. Still, a very rich compendium
    of information about all kinds of things OO that may broaden your horizons. Written
    by someone who was far too accepting of complexity, but also much more open to the
    diversity of opinions and forms than later mainstream practitioners would become, as the
    success of C++ and Java narrowed attention to a much smaller range of OO forms.
Carl Hewitt, Giuseppe Attardi, and Henry Lieberman. Security and Modularity in Mes-
    sage Passing. MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, AI-WP-180, 1979. https:
    //dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/41147 16 years before Rees 1995, the au-
    thors use an early capability-based security mechanism in their Actor system ACT1—by
    selectively granting users access to message constructors. They also implement both Pro-
    totype OO (under the name “delegation”, a mechanism “developed jointly with Kahn”,
    author of Director, cited). and Class OO (under the name “inheritance”). The delegation
    mechanism “increas[es] the modularity of the system”; classes allow “sharing of descrip-
    tions common to many actors”. When an actor delegates message handling to another,
    messages it does not handle itself are passed to the other actor wrapped in a “Buck_pass”
    message that reifies the message and its context. Cites Simula, Smalltalk and Director.
Carl Hewitt, Peter Bishop, and Richard Steiger. A Universal Modular ACTOR Formalism for
     Artificial Intelligence. In Nils J. Nilsson (Ed.), Proc. Proceedings of the 3rd International
     Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence, pp. 235–245. William Kaufmann, Los Altos,
     CA, USA, 1973. https://eighty-twenty.org/files/Hewitt,%20Bishop,%20St
     eiger%20-%201973%20-%20A%20universal%20modular%20ACTOR%20formalism%
     20for%20artificial%20intelligence.pdf The first published paper centered on
     the Actor model, following a December 1972 technical report. It unifies the formalism
     around the single concept of an ACTOR, an active object whose behavior is ultimately
     expressed by sending messages to other actors. Data structures, functions, processes and
368                                                       ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY

      many other computational entities are presented as special cases of actors.
Michael Hicks, Jonathan T. Moore, and Scott Nettles. Dynamic Software Updating. In Proc.
    ACM SIGPLAN 2001 Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementa-
    tion, PLDI ’01, pp. 13–23. Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA,
    2001. doi:10.1145/378795.378798. This seminal PLDI paper introduced one of the
    earliest practical, type-safe systems for dynamic software updating (DSU) in low-level
    languages like C, targeting long-running servers or systems that can’t afford downtime
    (e.g., web servers, routers, telecom switches). The proposed system automates a lot of
    the issues, but still relies on the programmer to insert explicit “safe update points”, so
    that upgrades shall only happen when the system has reached a “quiescent state”, and the
    upgrade shall not interfere catastrophically with running request handlers.
Hirrolot. awesome-c-preprocessor: A list of awesome C preprocessor stuff. 2021. https://
     github.com/Hirrolot/awesome-c-preprocessor (accessed 2026-02-09). GitHub
     repository containing a curated list of C preprocessor metaprogramming frameworks,
     extensions, interpreters, articles, and related resources. See notably hirrolot/metalang99
     or boostorg/preprocessor. If only I could trace the old hbaker USENET posts on this topic
     and see how far he got back then!
Florent Hivert and Nicolas M. Thiéry. Controlling the C3 Super Class Linearization Algorithm
     for Large Hierarchies of Classes. Order 41(1), pp. 83–98, 2024. https://arxiv.org/
     abs/2401.12740 The authors describe how they have automated the maintenance of C3
     consistency properties for the SageMath abstract algebra system since 2013, their system
     being large enough that manual consistency maintenance doesn’t scale. They notably
     use a clever instrumented C3 algorithm to output minimal local order specifications that
     will force for some new class a precedence list compatible with the desired global order
     between classes. The paper has a few minor technical defects (inaccurate propositions 1
     and 2, artificial implicit constraint on their problem 1), but they are of little consequence.
     and pale before the major practical achievement of getting such a large system to work.
C.A.R. Hoare. Record handling. Algol Bulletin 21, pp. 39–69, 1965. http://archive.
    computerhistory.org/resources/text/Knuth_Don_X4100/PDF_index/k-9
    -pdf/k-9-u2293-Record-Handling-Hoare.pdf This seminal paper introduces
    classes and subclasses, and many other notions now familiar and ubiquitous, including
    his infamous “million dollar mistake”, null. Hoare calls “objects” and “attributes” high-
    level entities being modeled, “classes” their types, “records” and “fields” the low-level
    representations of those as “consecutive words of computer store”, and “record classes”
    their types. “References” are typed pointers, and “null” is a special reference used when
    a correspondence is partial rather than total. “Discrimination” is a form of type-safe
    pattern-matching among subclasses. Hoare considers recursive data structures, yet does
    not anticipate that for them, subclassing will differ from subtyping.
C.A.R. Hoare. Null References: The Billion Dollar Mistake. 2009. https://www.infoq.
    com/presentations/Null-References-The-Billion-Dollar-Mistake-Ton
    y-Hoare (accessed 2026-02-04). Talk delivered at QCon London, August 2009. “I call
    it my billion-dollar mistake. It was the invention of the null reference in 1965.”

    work, and evaluates the resulting program against PyTorch using the GPU-targeting Co-

Daniel Ingalls. The evolution of Smalltalk: from Smalltalk-72 through Squeak. Proc.
    ACM Program. Lang. 4(HOPL), 2020. doi:10.1145/3386335. Dan Ingalls retreads
    the evolution of Smalltalk. Of particular interest to me was Ted Kaehler’s OOZE,
    the Object-Oriented Zoned Environment, an object-granular virtual memory system that
    made Smalltalk images orthogonally persistent between 1973 and 1978. Also evidence,
    if any was needed, that the word “Object-Oriented” was definitely in active use in Kay’s
    group in 1973 and earlier. But Ingalls also explains how Kay’s team was aspiring to
    “superclasses” and the yet-unnamed concept of inheritance in 1973 and probably earlier,
    though they only got them with Smalltalk-76. On the other hand, Ingalls states he started
    working on Smalltalk-76 in August 1976, so three months after KRL-0 was complete
    and one month after the KRL-0 paper was published. Thus Lisp (Interlisp) implemented
    inheritance (and thus proper, modern OO) before Smalltalk did.
Daniel H. H. Ingalls. The Smalltalk-76 Programming System: Design and Implementation. In
    Proc. the 5th ACM SIGACT-SIGPLAN Symposium on Principles of Programming Lan-

    USA, 1978. doi:10.1145/512760.512762. This very influential paper is the first formal
    paper about Smalltalk that uses the word “object-oriented”, describing Smalltalk-76, from

Bart Jacobs. Objects and Classes, Co-Algebraically. In Proc. Object Orientation with Par-
     allelism and Persistence, pp. 83–103, 1995. doi:10.5555/261075.261479. Cook pos-
     itively mentioned Jacobs in private email, and cites him in Cook 2012, as justification
     why OO doesn’t need inheritance. But this paper is actually not OO at all, it is relational
     modeling with Category Theory. In the last paragraph of section 2, Jacobs says that “Ai,
     Bi, Ci are (constant) sets.” All the negation of actual OO is concentrated in this single
     word hidden between parentheses, lost in the middle of the article, that restricts classes
     to the non-recursive subset where the NNOOTT applies. Wow. But that doesn’t require
     malice, only ignorance. Jacobs cites Goguen, who was also using Category Theory; but
     Goguen was using it to do rewrite logic and software specification with the trappings of
     OO. Jacobs does just relational data modeling. Jacobs can be partly forgiven for straying
     out of his usual domain and wrongly trusting apparent authorities (Goguen). Cook can-
     not be forgiven for spreading nonsense precisely on the domain in which he sought and
370                                                     ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY

      acquired authority.

Anita Jones and Barbara Liskov. A Language Extension for Controlling Access to Shared
    Data. IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering SE-2(4), pp. 277–285, 1976.
    doi:10.1109/TSE.1976.233833. Also MIT CSG Memo 137 from April 1976, this is
    one of the very first papers using the words “object-oriented”, and AFAICT the very first
    one to do it with a definition. However, this not a definition that I, or much anyone else,
    accept, since J&L have it mean, in my words, modularity but without extensibility, what
    Wegner calls “object-based”.
        J&L cite Simula 67, CLU and Alphard as their examples of OO, but not Smalltalk
    (maybe for lack of publication to cite). Simula is a good example, but Alphard is just
    hopeless vaporware, and the authors’ language CLU is at the forefront of internal mod-
    ularity but completely ignores internal extensibility. J&L also cite Lisp, but only in the
    context of already offering the kind of functionality they use as a code example. Their
    not including it among their examples of OO is correct, since KRL wasn’t a part of Lisp
    but an extension on top of it—and was published later.
        Still, a good paper, with some of CLU’s great contributions to the topic of modularity.

Kenneth Michael Kahn. An Actor-Based Computer Animation Language. In Proc.
    ACM/SIGGRAPH Workshop on User-Oriented Design of Interactive Graphics Sys-
    tems, UODIGS ’76, pp. 37–43. Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY,
    USA, 1976. doi:10.1145/1024273.1024278. Kahn describes his yet unnamed language
    inspired by Hewitt’s actors (PLASMA) and Smalltalk-72, which would evolve into the
    language later called “Director”. In modern terms it is prototype-based, though Kahn
    himself uses class-and-instance terminology for what, in modern terms, is a prototype-

Kenneth Michael Kahn. Creation of computer animation from story descriptions. PhD disser-
    tation, MIT, 1979a. https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/16012 This thesis
    is about the higher-level system Ani, which generates turtle graphics plans on top of the
    actor-based object system Director (see AIM-482b). Ani is a constraint solver based on a
    knowledge representation of the film being directed: a very crude 2D film with polygons
    as "performers" that move toward, away from, around or between one another, at various
    speeds appropriate to the action, as humans would on a stage. Kahn cites Bobrow &

Kenneth Michael Kahn. Director Guide. MIT, AIM-482b, 1979b. https://dspace.mit.e
    du/handle/1721.1/6302 This paper, revised from a previous 1978 edition, presents
    Director, the earliest Lisp OO programming system as such, where inheritance exists in
    a programming context, not just in the knowledge representation context from which it
    evolved; see Kahn 1976. By then, Director had been factored out as the actor language
    underlying Kahn’s wider animation project Ani. Director implements single inheritance
    by passing unhandled messages to a parent actor, with the initial receiver’s identity as
    first argument. An actor knows its parent, offspring, descendants, siblings and childless-
    descendants as special variables (only the word “ancestor” does not appear). Director has
    an early form of call-next-method called continue-asking (p.40). The Actor team would
    later adapt Kahn’s inheritance mechanism under the name “delegation”; see Hewitt 1979.
    Kahn cites Smalltalk and Actors as influences for Director, but not KRL (Kahn does cite
    KRL in his thesis).
Samuel N. Kamin. Inheritance in Smalltalk-80: A Denotational Definition. In Proc. POPL,
   1988. doi:10.1145/73560.73567. With Reddy 1988, one of the very first formal seman-
   tics for OO, with a simplified static model of Smalltalk-80 with single inheritance. Kamin
   uses syntactic rewrite rules, that he directly translated into a running ML program. This
   paper deserves much praise for being a first of its genre, translating a foreign paradigm
   in the vocabulary of FP, and being constructive with an actual running implementation
   based on U-encoding. In a way, the paper does too much by trying to have a realistic
   subset of Smalltalk, and too little by spending too little time explaining its dense model
   of inheritance, indeed as the fixpoint of the hierarchy of class definitions. But that’s OK,
   because Reddy 1988 is a very complementary paper that explains the concepts behind
   Kamin.
Samuel N. Kamin and Uday S. Reddy. Two Semantic Models of Object-Oriented Lan-
   guages. In Theoretical Aspects of Object-Oriented Programming: Types, Semantics,
   and Language Design Chapter 13, Carl A. Gunter and John C. Mitchell (Ed.), Foun-
   dations of Computing, pp. 463–496. The MIT Press, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 1994.
   https://openlibrary.org/books/OL1419064M/Theoretical_aspects_o
372                                                        ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY

      f_object-oriented_programming Kamin and Reddy join forces once again after
      their famous 1988 papers, and explicitly compare updated versions of their two semantic
      models of OO. The paper is heavy on formalism, which in the end drowns rather than
      highlights its beautiful conclusion: the equivalence between what they finally call the
      fixed-point model and the self-application model—what in this book I call Y-encoding
      and U-encoding.
           I feel the paper is important enough that it deserves my nitpicking everything wrong
      about it—because, when stripped from those inessential mistakes, the paper really shines
      for its essential achievement.
           As for the complexity of the paper: the authors independently implement classes in
      both models, rather than factoring out their common specification machinery, which re-
      quires two separate layers of scaffolding whose equivalence must then be proved. My pre-
      sentation is much simpler for accepting specifications as more fundamental than classes;
      equivalence between the two encodings becomes trivial, and the scaffolding for classes
      on top of specifications can be built once and shared between encodings.
           Also, Kamin and Reddy for most of the paper call the two models respectively “clo-
      sure semantics” and “data structure semantics”, because the Y-encoding of Reddy 1988,
      like those of Cook 1987 and my chapter 5, involves representing records as functions (clo-
      sures) so as to directly invoke a fixpoint operator, whereas the U-encoding from Kamin
      1988, like most low-level implementations all the way back to Sutherland 1963, rep-
      resents objects as records of instance variables plus a reference to the type descriptor
      containing the methods, where each method is explicitly passed the record as argument.
           But this is a trivial accident of their models, independent of the essential distinction
      between Y-encoding and U-encoding. Steels 1983 shows you can do U-encoding with
      closures whereas my Rideau 2020 shows you can do Y-encoding with records. (And
      Abelson 1984 shows you can have records-as-closures without either Y- or U-encoding.)
      Note that Kiselyov 2005 and Simons 2015 also do kind of Y-encoding with records, but
      both use lazy languages, where recursively defined values of any type, including records,
      are considerably easier to construct, making that less remarkable than it sounds. In any
      case, they get the naming right in the end—but I want the reader to avoid being misled by
      this accident.
           Finally, the authors claim that Y-encoding is more abstract than U-encoding. I admit I
      thought so too at first, but surprisingly they are wrong to generalize from the particular se-
      mantic domains of their separately constructed class models to the encodings themselves:
      purely local transformations can translate between the two encodings at the level of open
      object specifications, independently of any class scaffolding built on top of them. Thus,
      neither encoding is intrinsically more abstract than the other. Recovering these transfor-
      mations is left as a fun exercise to the reader (solutions are available in pommette, the
      code accompanying this book).
Mark Kantrowitz. Portable Utilities for Common Lisp. School of Computer Science,
    Carnegie-Mellon University, CMU-CS-91-143, 1991. https://cl- pdx.com/sta
    tic/CMU-CS-91-143.pdf A collection of portable free software utilities in Common
    Lisp, among which the first non-proprietary reimplementation of DEFSYSTEM (later
    known as MK-DEFSYSTEM to distinguish it from others), the only one until ASDF.
    Making the code portable across platforms that are not very well-defined with respect to
    files and processes, without a well-compartmentalized portability layer, makes for a lot
    of bad corner cases, and is difficult to refactor after the live knowledge of what exactly
    the code is supposed to mean is gone. So after Mark stopped maintaining, it was hard for
    maintainer to handle the bitrot, leading to a reimplementation from scratch, ASDF (for
ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY                                                                   373

    which I separated and documented a well-defined portability layer).
Alan Kay. The Early History of Smalltalk. In History of programming languages—II 28(3),
    pp. 511–598. Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 1993.
    doi:10.1145/155360.155364. Great read about Smalltalk. Inheritance is discussed in
    section 11.5.1: Simula-style inheritance was deliberately left out of Kay’s work on FLEX
    and early Smalltalk. Kay credits Larry Tesler (slot inheritance), Henry Lieberman (del-
    egation), and Bobrow and Winograd’s KRL (Frames), for the invention of Smalltalk in-
    heritance.

Gregor Kiczales, Jim Des Rivières, and Daniel G. Bobrow. The Art of the Meta-Object Pro-
    tocol. MIT Press, 1991. https://direct.mit.edu/books/book/2607/The-Art
    -of-the-Metaobject-Protocol This classic book, often known as AMOP, describes
    how the implementation of an OO system can itself use OO, making it extensible using
    itself, which can be used both for richer semantics and higher performance. The feat re-
    quires a few manually tied loops to bootstrap the system. Beautiful. Many Common Lisp

    from the Common Lisp standard itself.

    540-45337-7_18. The canonical reference for AspectJ, the most widely adopted AOP

Gregor Kiczales, John Lamping, Anurag Mendhekar, Chris Maeda, Cristina Videira Lopes,
    Jean-Marc Loingtier, and John Irwin. Aspect-Oriented Programming. In Proc.
    ECOOP’97 — Object-Oriented Programming, 11th European Conference, Jyväskylä,
    Finland, June 9-13, 1997, Lecture Notes in Computer Science, 1241, pp. 220–242.
    Springer, 1997. doi:10.1007/BFb0053381. This is the original, defining paper for
    Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP). It introduced the key ideas of cross-cutting con-
    cerns, aspects, join points, advice, and aspect weaving. Cross-cutting aspects are exactly
374                                                      ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY

      what create combinatorial pressure on single inheritance, and can be solved with multiple

Roger King. My Cat Is Object-Oriented. In Object-Oriented Concepts, Databases, and Ap-
    plications Chapter 2, Won Kim and Frederick H. Lochovsky (Ed.), ACM Press Fron-
    tier Series, pp. 23–30. ACM Press and Addison-Wesley, New York, NY, USA, 1989.
    doi:10.1145/63320.66469. King mocks loose definitions of OO based on random de-
    sirable properties, using the deliberately absurd example of classifying his cat as object-

Oleg Kiselyov and Ralf Lämmel. Haskell’s overlooked object system. 2005. https:
    //arxiv.org/abs/cs/0509027 The magical Oleg shows that, actually, there is enough
    structural subtyping hidden in the Haskell typesystem to do precisely the kind of things
    people usually do with OO, with lists of types at the type-level to handle extensible record
    types. Though Oleg does not bother to implement multiple inheritance, some have imple-
    mented Quicksort at the type-level in Haskell, so topological sort with C4 is probably just
    some more type astronautics away. As compared to most OO papers that discuss theory
    only, or push their own ad hoc system, Oleg discusses pragmatics, and reuses someone
    else’s language, without having to change it, all by programming at the type-level. On
    the other hand, Oleg is well versed in the theory precisely because he does his practical
    work decades after the theorists wrote their papers.
Shriram Krishnamurthi. Programming Languages: Application and Interpretation. 1st edi-
     tion. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, USA, 2008. https://plai.org/ This
     is a great book about Programming Languages in general, and I love SK. SK introduces
     objects as closures, and even prototypes, in chapter 10. But one thing he just doesn’t get
     is multiple inheritance (10.3.3). In 10.3.5 he introduces mixins as a mechanism on top of
     first-class single-inheritance classes, which certainly works, but to me feels like putting
     the cart before the ox. Great stuff outside OO, and even the OO is decent, but in the end,
     like many academics, SK doesn’t grok OO. (The third edition has some improvements,
     but is still not there.)
Bent Bruun Kristensen, Ole Lehrmann Madsen, Birger Møller-Pedersen, and Kristen Ny-
    gaard. The BETA programming language. Department of Computer Science, Aarhus
    University, DAIMI PB-229, 1987. doi:10.7146/dpb.v16i229.7578. BETA is the suc-
    cessor of Simula. It claims to unify classes, procedures, functions and types as a single
    abstraction mechanism called “patterns”. Patterns are restricted prototypes that conflate
    first-class target records-or-procedures with second-class specifications of those targets
    that can be used with single inheritance (later work by Agesen et al. 1989 would make
    BETA specifications first class too, and the successor gBeta (Ernst 2000) would further
    expand the semantics of records into prototypes with dynamic (mutable) inheritance).
         A “do” body is executed when an object of the pattern is invoked, with inputs bound
    to variables from an “enter” part (if any), and outputs are computed from expressions
    specified by an “exit” part (if any). Multiple invocations of a given object will overwrite
ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY                                                                      375

    the enter variables and execute the body anew, and so the expected way to use a pattern
    P as a function is to invoke a new object &P at each function call, making the analogy
    between object and call frame tangible.
         Inheritance works by extending a pattern and, recursively, any virtual subpatterns
    further-bound along with it, at each level generalizing Simula’s concatenation seman-
    tics: in each “do” block, an “inner” keyword may specify where to execute a subpattern’s
    additional “do” code (if there is no “inner”, then any descendant-provided code will be ig-
    nored and never executed, which is unlike Simula, and an improvement in this context). In
    BETA, ancestors control the execution of descendants’ extensions, whereas in other lan-
    guages, descendants’ extensions override and control the execution of ancestor-provided
    code. BETA patterns are open recursive, and this(P) denotes the current P object when
    used within P or code lexically nested inside P, while “inner P” can execute descendant-
    provided body extensions. Ugly: any communication of information between descendant
    and ancestor “do” blocks must happen through side effects to lexically shared variables.
         Particularly remarkable is the treatment of how inheritance interacts with lexical nest-
    ing of patterns (which generalizes to prototypes and classes in other languages): “virtual
    patterns” partake of the specialization structure of their enclosing pattern (unlike “pattern
    variables” later introduced—an is-a vs has-a distinction). The semantic infrastructure to
    do it right already existed in earlier prototype languages such as KRL or Act-1; but their
    authors don’t seem to have specifically noticed and examined the semantics of nested
    prototypes. The BETA team did it first, and the author of the successor gBeta gave under-
    standable explanations of the phenomenon as “family polymorphism” (Ernst 2001). Un-
    happily, this achievement is mired by the authors trying to bolt an incoherent type theory
    on top of it: inspired by the absurd premise that subclassing is subtyping (the NNOOTT),
    further binding specializes virtual patterns monotonically (correct) but BETA simulta-
    neously treats specialization of the enclosing pattern as subtyping (incorrect); thus if a
    virtual pattern occurs in an input position, the result is required to be covariant parameter
    specialization, which is absurd. Meanwhile their typechecker unifies types it shouldn’t by
    failing to distinguish between the same pattern instantiated in different enclosing objects
    and hence distinct lexical environments (e.g. x.V vs y.V). Ernst addresses these typing
    issues in gBeta.
         The report is hard to read: the authors are in their own world, with their own vocabu-
    lary, syntax and semantics, and fail to try to reduce their semantics to something simple in
    terms of logic, or anything understandable by others. Nygaard, Kristensen, Madsen and
    soon Møller-Pedersen started the BETA project in 1976, when others already had better
    OO (except, it bears repeating, with regard to nested patterns). By the time their design
    stabilized around 1980, they were far behind the OO state of the art, and they never caught
    up with progress that came up after 1977. Quite underwhelming. They never entered a
    mutually beneficial dialogue with the rest of the OO world, wherein they could exchange
    ideas in a common formalism, import good ideas from others, export good ideas from
    them. Very sad waste of great talent by self-imposed intellectual isolation.
         Also published in Shriver & Wegner (eds.), Research Directions in Object-Oriented
    Programming, MIT Press, 1987, pp. 7–48.
Stein Krogdahl. Multiple Inheritance in Simula-like Languages. BIT Numerical Mathemat-
     ics 25(2), pp. 318–326, 1985. doi:10.1007/BF01934377. Krogdahl extends Simula’s
     single-inheritance “prefix” mechanism to support multiple prefixes... but only for tree-
     shaped ancestries. Quite lame, especially since he cites both Borning and Cannon who
     did much better years earlier. He’s not even trying. But at least he doesn’t try to explode
     DAGs into trees like C++. This 1985 extension is obviously not part of Simula 67; it was
376                                                       ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY

      not included in the 1986 Simula Standard, either, which retained single inheritance.
Butler W. Lampson. Hints for Computer System Design. In Proc. Proceedings of the
    9th ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, pp. 33–48. ACM, 1983.
    doi:10.1145/800217.806614. A collection of practical principles for designing com-
    puter systems, distilled from Lampson’s experience at Xerox PARC and elsewhere.
Julia L. Lawall and Daniel P. Friedman. Embedding the Self Language in Scheme. Com-
     puter Science Department, Indiana University, TR-276, 1989. https://scholarwor
     ks.iu.edu/dspace/items/73ab556f-b16e-42df-859d-da17f3ddcef6 This
     paper re-implements the prototype object system of Self in Scheme, thereby making its
     semantics more understandable. This notably includes mutable slots, cloning, mutable
     inheritance, method resolution depth-first without backtracking along the what Ungar
     calls the “sender path”. If the result doesn’t look quite so simple after all, it is because
     Self isn’t as simple conceptually as it aims to be; authors confuse length of low-level
     code for ease of reasoning at a high-level. A prototype object system in Scheme can be
     vastly simpler to implement as well as reason about (see T and YASOS, or the code in
     this book).
Primo Levi. Se questo è un uomo. De Silva, 1947. This book impressed me when I read it
    as a young man (in a French translation), and the words “Hier ist kein warum!” (Here
    there is no why!) still haunt me: the reply of a guard who snatched an icicle from the
    desperately thirsty Levi when he asked why. A 1959 translation to English by Stuart
    Woolf was published as “If this is a man”, or in US editions “Survival in Auschwitz”.
Henry Lieberman. Using Prototypical Objects to Implement Shared Behavior in Object-
    Oriented Systems. In Proc. Proceedings of the 1986 ACM Conference on Object-
    Oriented Programming Systems, Languages and Applications (OOPSLA ’86), pp.
    214–223. Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 1986.
    doi:10.1145/28697.28718. This is a rightly influential paper about Prototype OO,
    as compared to Class OO.
         Lieberman starts with the philosophical underpinnings of these two complexes of
    ideas, which are quite interesting from a historical and psychological point of view, but
    have little relevance to a technical discussion decades later on the semantics of OO, its
    proper use or implementation. He then contrasts how the two OO paradigms are typi-
    cally used to represent knowledge, how they compare in expressiveness, efficiency, con-
    currency issues and suitability for interactive use. He even explains (section 6) how to
    implement inheritance (i.e. Classes) in terms of delegation (i.e. Prototypes) and why a
    correspondence in the other direction is impossible (because inheritance depends only on
    the class, known before the instance is bound; the same argument as my “inheritance hap-
    pens only at compile-time for 2nd-class classes, whereas prototypes need it at runtime”,
    but with a finer-grained staging of computation “times”).
         Sadly, this great paper has been largely cited for the one bad take of its author: Lieber-
    man unhelpfully identifies Prototype OO and Class OO with the respective underlying
    “delegation” and “inheritance” mechanisms, rather than distinguishing the nature of the
    targets of otherwise identical specification mechanisms.
Barbara Liskov. Data Abstraction and Hierarchy. In Proc. OOPSLA ’87, pp. 17–34. ACM,
    1987. doi:10.1145/62138.62141. In her invited talk at OOPSLA, Liskov in section 3
    promptly dismissed inheritance of implementation as “violating encapsulation”, a quick
    hack that doesn’t fit her semantic model focused on subtyping. She obviously does not
    understand the purpose and semantics on inheritance, falls deep into the NNOOTT, and
    with inheritance of implementation dismisses any actual OO. And yet, the same paper
ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY                                                                    377

    first introduces a variant of her now famous “Liskov substitution principle”. So, is it a
    bad paper? Was it wrong to invite her at OOPSLA? Not at all. She is a great influential
    researcher who deserved her Turing Award. But was her talk good about OO? Not at all
    either. It was a good talk at OOPSLA, just not one about OO.
Barbara Liskov. A History of CLU. In Jr. Thomas J. Bergin and Jr. Richard G. Gibson
    (Ed.), Proc. History of Programming Languages—II, pp. 471–510. ACM, New York,
    NY, USA, 1993. doi:10.1145/154766.155367. Liskov’s retrospective account of the
    development of data abstraction and CLU (previously MIT LCS-TR-561 report from
    1992). It presents CLU as the first implemented language providing direct linguistic
    support for data abstraction and discusses its relationship to the distinct object-oriented
    tradition. Liskov is careful to distinguish her meaning for object-oriented (Wegner’s and
    my “object-based”) under which CLU is OO, from what she reckons is the more common
    meaning that includes inheritance.
William M. Lonergan and Paul A. King. Design of the B5000 System. Datamation 7(5), pp.
     28–32, 1961. https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~kubitron/courses/cs
     252-S12/handouts/papers/b5000.pdf The paper presents the Burroughs B5000
     computer architecture, one of the sources of inspiration cited by Alan Kay. It features a
     push-down stack (with “right-hand” Polish notation, prefiguring FORTH’s stack/RPN ex-
     ecution model); “independence of addressing” (memory position-independence for both
     code and data) through a “program reference table” (a relocatable table of values and
     descriptors for indirect access to data and program segments, prefiguring later linkage
     tables and, more distantly, some of the indirection mechanisms used for object dispatch,
     as well as execution environments and capability namespaces).
Augusta Ada Lovelace. Notes [on translation of Luigi Federico Menabrae’s paper on Bab-
   bage’s Analytical Engine]. In Richard Taylor’s Scientific Memoirs pp. 666–731. Richard
   and John E. Taylor, 1843. https://www.google.com/books/edition/Scienti
   fic_Memoirs_Selected_from_the_Tra/qsY-AAAAYAAJ?gbpv=1&pg=PA666 This
   paper is verily the foundation of all Computer Science, which should rightfully be called
   by the name Lovelace baptized it: “the science of operations”.
        Ada Augusta King, Countess of Lovelace, translates to English an article (in French)
   about the Babbage Analytical Engine, by Luigi Menabrea, who would later become Prime
   Minister of newly unified Italy; and her translator’s notes are fantastic. Only her initials
   appear (A.A.L, at one point mistyped A.L.L.), because a woman, especially a noble one,
   shall not write, especially not on such lowly topics. But my! Her understanding of
   “operations”, the general notion of pure computation, is better than that of most computer
   scientists of today.
        “First the symbols of operation are frequently also the symbols of the results of op-
   erations. We may say that symbols are apt to have both a retrospective and a prospective
   signification. [. . . ]” She groks both that there is a conflation of multiple meanings, and
   that it is good, yet can lead to confusion if not made explicit: past vs future, passive vs
   active, values vs continuations. She also anticipates symbolic computing: “symbolical”
   vs “numerical” “results” or “data” (outputs or inputs); and the dual use of symbols as
   code and data: “the symbols of numerical magnitude, are frequently also the symbols of
   operations”.
        She understands that programmability (she lacks the word) makes the Analytical en-
   gine vastly superior to the fixed-purpose Difference Engine, indeed makes it “the execu-
   tive right hand of abstract algebra”. She also confronts the problem that a variable may
   take multiple values during an execution, and proposes an elegant solution, using a su-
378                                                      ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY

      perscript to the left of a variable to number each successive binding, turning them into
      actual mathematical variables again. Way more advanced than most computer scientists
      even today. Prescient.
Yuri I. Manin. Mathematics as Metaphor. American Mathematical Society, 2007.
    doi:10.1093/philmat/nkn013. This collection of writings about mathematics includes a
    nice Foreword by Freeman Dyson.
Scott Meyers. Effective C++: 50 Specific Ways to Improve Your Programs and Designs.
    Addison-Wesley Professional Computing Series. Addison-Wesley, Reading, MA, USA,
    1992. An influential collection of design and programming guidelines for how to use
    C++. Solid practical advice, rooted in language knowledge and experience, at the right
    level of abstraction for users of the language. At times, theory could have helped sim-
    plify the discourse, but the book is consistent in its style and level of abstraction, which
    is overall more valuable. Its chapter on “Inheritance and Object-Oriented Design” is of
    a similar caliber: solid, practical, no-nonsense, based on solid understanding of the lan-
    guage, without taking sides on theoretical debates. It explicitly distinguishes public in-
    heritance as modeling an “isa” relationship from “layering” (what others call aggregation
    or composition) as modeling either “has-a” or “is-implemented-in-terms-of”. The differ-
    ence between the latter being that “has-a” cleanly exports the component and its interface
    as a member, whereas “is-implemented-in-terms-of” is about a hidden internal choice of
    representation that does not export its interface and could be replaced. Meyers explains
    that private inheritance in C++ is another way to model “is-implemented-in-terms-of”.
Matthew Might, Yannis Smaragdakis, and David Van Horn. Resolving and exploiting the
    k-CFA paradox: illuminating functional vs. object-oriented program analysis. In Proc.
    Proceedings of the 31st ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Programming Language Design
    and Implementation, PLDI ’10, pp. 305–315. Association for Computing Machinery,
    New York, NY, USA, 2010. doi:10.1145/1806596.1806631. The authors note how
    the complexity of k-CFA (Control Flow Analysis with context of depth k) was proven
    EXPTIME-complete for FP, yet polynomial for OOP; they then explain the difference as
    actually being about treatment of scopes, that are flattened by the requirement in typi-
    cal OO languages that closures be created by explicitly creating objects with plenty of
    variables at once, when in FP (especially so with curried functions) you may get an expo-
    nential number of abstract nested closure values per number of variables. The flattened
    environment representation in OOP loses precision in exchange for a gain in execution
    speed. The same representation is possible in FP, using flattened environments rather than
    shared DAGs of scopes. From an abstract argument about complexity, the authors thus
    identify concrete improvements to algorithms for program representation and analysis.
    The correspondence between program analysis, abstract interpretation, and typesystems,
    may also suggest how this affects the complexity of types for OO in a closed program
    being optimized vs an open program being extended.
Marvin Minsky. A Framework for Representing Knowledge. MIT, AIM-306, 1974. http
    s://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/6089 Minsky describes his ideas on how
    to represent knowledge in a computer as part of his project for Artificial Intelligence,
    in terms of structured “frames” representing stereotyped situations, linked into frame-
    systems and containing slots, defaults and procedural information. Minsky even uses the
    words “prototype” and “inherit”, but entirely incidentally, and NOT AT ALL to refer to
    the concepts at stake for OO.

John C. Mitchell and Gordon D. Plotkin. Abstract Types have Existential Type. In Proc. Pro-
    ceedings of the 12th ACM Symposium on Principles of Programming Languages (POPL
    ’85), pp. 37–51, 1985. doi:10.1145/318593.318606. The title of this key paper captures
    the core contribution: implementations of abstract data types, consisting of a representa-
    tion type and operations on it (i.e. modules), can hide their actual representation type you
    should think of abstract types for data and functions that operate on them (i.e. modules)
    as hiding the actual underlying type behind an existential quantifier. This enables reason-
    ing about modules as first-class values in a second-order 𝜆-calculus. An extended journal
    version was published in TOPLAS 10(3), 1988.
Torben Ægidius Mogensen.          Self-Applicable Online Partial Evaluation of the Pure
    Lambda-Calculus.         In Proc.      1995 ACM SIGPLAN Symposium on Partial
    Evaluation and Semantics-Based Program Manipulation, pp.                    39–44, 1995.
    doi:10.1145/215465.215469. M encodes of the 𝜆-calculus in itself using higher-
    order syntax, then has interpreters, reducers and partial evaluators for the encoding, and
    Futamura projections for those partial evaluators, and interactions with the Y combinator.
    Very cool stuff. Not directly related to OO, though. Also the representation choosen
    deliberately does not expose the sharing or non-sharing of nodes during graph reduction
    and evaluation; it is a “shallow” encoding in this way, which is actually great for many
    applications (where these details are a bore), and terrible for other applications (where
    these details are crucial).
Eugenio Moggi. Notions of computation and monads. Information and computation 93(1), pp.
    55–92, 1991. doi:10.1016/0890-5401(91)90052-4. This seminal paper that explains how
    computations with all kinds of side effects can be expressed on top of the pure 𝜆-calculus
    using monads. Though presented as an abstract tool for reasoning about the semantics
    of programming languages, the technique would quickly be adapted as the concrete basis
    for how Haskell exposes side effects indeed. Math heavy with category theory diagrams.
David A. Moon. Object-Oriented Programming with Flavors. SIGPLAN Not. 21(11), pp. 1–8,
    1986. doi:10.1145/960112.28698. According to Gabriel 2012, this was “the first engi-
    neering publication about mixins” (in the Lisp sense, as introduced by Flavors), whereas
    Cannon’s 1979 report (this paper cites a 1982 copy) was privately circulated, mostly in
    Lisp circles at MIT and beyond (however, the Lisp Machine Manual from 1981 onward
    includes a chapter on Flavors).
        This paper describes the New Flavors system from Symbolics, after it acquired the
    new “generic function” syntax, respect for local precedence order, and other niceties.
    Moon rightfully insists on the modularity advantage of Flavors (already mentioned by
    Cannon). This is a fantastic explanation of how to do multiple inheritance right, only
    way too short.
Oscar Nierstrasz. Ten Things I Hate About Object-Oriented Programming. Journal of Object
    Technology 9(5), pp. 5–16, 2010. doi:10.5381/jot.2010.9.5.e1. Nierstrasz is an OOP
    researcher in the Smalltalk tradition. In this provocative essay, he criticizes a few things
    about how OO is commonly practiced. The criticism is not always about OO itself,
    though sometimes it is; and whether it hits or misses, it certainly brings challenging
    thoughts and can inspire directions for future R&D.
Martin Odersky and Matthias Zenger. Scalable component abstractions. In Proc. 20th Annual
    ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Object-Oriented Programming, Systems, Languages, and
    Applications, OOPSLA ’05, 40(10), pp. 41–57. Association for Computing Machinery,
    New York, NY, USA, 2005. doi:10.1145/1103845.1094815. This paper describes the
    OO and FP model of Scala 2 (then being developed), its flavorful multiple inheritance
380                                                      ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY

      and its typesystem, with self-types and recursive type constraints. Imperfect as it may be
      (e.g. lack of C3, proper tail calls, and compromises to fit Java and the JVM), Scala has
      by far the best integration of OO, FP and types.
Chris Okasaki. Purely Functional Data Structures. PhD dissertation, Carnegie Mellon Univer-
    sity, Pittsburgh, PA, 1996. https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~rwh/students/okasaki.
    pdf Okasaki’s PhD thesis, his original presentation of persistent purely functional data
    structures based on structural sharing and amortized analysis. It was later expanded into
    a great 1998 book with same title. A classic, greatly recommended.
Chris Okasaki and Andy Gill. Fast Mergeable Integer Maps. In Proc. Proceedings of the ACM
    SIGPLAN Workshop on ML, pp. 77–86, 1998. http://www.ittc.ku.edu/csdl/f
    pg/files/Okasaki-98-IntMap.pdf Original paper for a pure functional variant of
    big-endian Patricia tree (a.k.a. trie), an efficient and popular way to represent finite maps
    indexed by integers (that themselves could be the values of a hash function).
Bruno C. d. S. Oliveira. The Different Aspects of Monads and Mixins. Oxford University
    Computing Laboratory, 2009. https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/publications/pub
    lication2965- abstract.html Oliveira shows that there is enough subtyping in
    Haskell typeclasses for cool applications of Mixins, even without resorting to the type
    astronautics of Kiselyov 2005 or Gale 2015. A very nice paper on Mixins, though short
    of being capable of typing OO.
Harold Ossher and William Harrison. Combination of Inheritance Hierarchies. In Proc. Con-
    ference Proceedings on Object-Oriented Programming Systems, Languages, and Appli-
    cations, OOPSLA ’92, pp. 25–40. Association for Computing Machinery, New York,
    NY, USA, 1992. doi:10.1145/141936.141940. The authors present the point of view of
    OO as being used to extend not just individual classes, but class hierarchies. They call
    “extension-as-addition” what I call extensibility, or maybe modular extensibility (unclear
    which, but in the end what they extend are indeed modular entities, classes and class
    hierarchies). They discuss strategies to avoid “conflict” between independent extensions.

    ACM 15(12), pp. 1053–1058, 1972. doi:10.1145/361598.361623. A truly classic paper
    on modularity and the source of the information-hiding criterion: decompose a system

Benjamin C. Pierce and David N. Turner. Simple Type-Theoretic Foundations for Object-
    Oriented Programming. 1993. https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/jour
    nal-of-functional-programming/article/simple-typetheoretic-foundat
    ions-for-objectoriented-programming/5C18E2E055B028F7214FBB183701830
    E This is a solid paper worth reading, though I staunchly disagree with both the “Simple”
    and “Foundations” in the title. Pierce and Turner do not provide solid foundations that
    pin-point the essence of all OO, based on which to build any OO system. Instead, they
    show how you can side-step some of the really hard problems in OO (recursive types!),
    yet achieve most of the value in practice, using existential types for modularity: they push
    the problematic fixpoint into a corner, and ask the user to tie the knot manually in a case
    where it’s relatively easy for the user to do; then their system handles the rest and does
    the heavy lifting from there. Users can then achieve most of the benefits of OO despite
    the system being unable to tie the knot and solve the problem automatically. It is a “tell
    me what you need, I’ll show you how to do without!” kind of paper. And you shouldn’t
382                                                        ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY

      take this description disparagingly: this is a great kind of paper, one that shows you how
      to do more with less. Brilliant and insightful. Yet, ultimately, an utter failure at the task

John C. Reynolds. Three Approaches to Type Structure. In Proc. Mathematical Foundations

    pp. 97–138. Springer, 1985. doi:10.1007/3-540-15198-2_7. Reynolds notes the equiva-

François-René Rideau. LIL: CLOS Reaches Higher-Order, Sheds Identity and has a Trans-
    formative Experience. In Proc. International Lisp Conference, 2012. http://github
    .com/fare/lil-ilc2012/ I show how to achieve parametric polymorphism in Com-
    mon Lisp, by passing around “interfaces”, objects that describe some API. Interfaces are
    analogous to the “dictionaries” with which typeclasses are implemented in Haskell, or
    to first-class ML modules, except they integrate very well with the OO capabilities of
    CLOS. I then show not only how to write either “pure” or “stateful” variants of such
    interfaces, but how the two are equivalent, and can be automatically transformed into
    one another with macros. Similarly, macros can automatically transform between these
    “pure” or “stateful” interface in typeclass styles and respective “posh” or “classy” classes
    in traditional OO style. Typeclass vs class, pure vs stateful are then just a matter of
    expression style rather than of fundamentally different computing paradigms.
François-René Rideau. ASDF 3, or Why Lisp is Now an Acceptable Scripting Language. In

    this paper, I describe the build system ASDF, and its design, its evolution from ASDF 1
    (and its predecessors) to ASDF 3, with surprising challenges from portability to extension
    of project scope, to a bug that was half-fixed in one line of code but required a complete
    rewrite for a real fix. The heart of ASDF is a protocol using plenty of multi-methods
    specialized on an operation and a component. The combination of flavorful multiple
    inheritance and multiple dispatch makes for an extremely modular and extensible design,
    that accomplishes in a few thousands of lines what other build systems do in tens or
    hundreds of thousands of lines of code.

François-René Rideau. Reconciling Semantics and Reflection. 2018b. https://bit.ly
    /FarePhD Unpublished because undefended. First draft completed in 2018, yet still
    not in a publishable state as of 2026. In my thesis, I reconcile Semantics (knowing as
    much as possible about the meaning of a program before you even run it, which might
    not terminate) and Reflection (being able to modify a program and its meaning while
    it’s running), two seemingly antinomic concepts—by developing a protocol to negotiate
    what can be changed and what must be preserved about a given program. Thus, users
    can trust the integrity of the software they use, developers can debug the most difficult
    situations and update the software as needed, and administrators can ensure the software
    runs on affordable and reliable hardware, even as requirements evolve, computers age and
    economic conditions change. The thesis distinguishes three orthogonal axes of “reflec-
    tion” that people commonly conflate or confuse: pre/post (code generation), hypo/hyper
    (semantic implementation), back/fore (runtime control). The thesis has four parts: The
    first part focuses on the notion of implementation, and the good properties one might
    expect from an implementation; one property is particularly important that everyone else
    neglects: observability. The second part shows how the same properties, well formalized,
    become a protocol for runtime reflection, wherein observability does the heavy lifting of
    synchronizing the system in a quiescent state that makes transformations possible. The
    third part explores what kind of existing practices can be simplified when explained in
    terms of such reflection protocol. The fourth part proposes a software architecture for
    reflective runtime control of software, based on the previous. The first two sound boring
    or trivial without the last two; the last two sound fantastic or impossible without the first
    two. And yet, the end result sounds simple and necessary once you have shifted your
    point of view from the common wisdom (or lack thereof) that most people induce from
    standard practice.
François-René Rideau. Gerbil-POO. 2020. https://github.com/fare/gerbil-poo
    (accessed 2021-04-06). A simple Prototype Object System on top of Gerbil Scheme, with
    flavorful multiple inheritance, in a mostly pure functional lazy style, yet also allowing for
    mutable state (though without support for dynamic changes in inheritance hierarchy). I
    implemented it initially as an exercise after discovering the Nix extension system, as a
    demonstration of how an object system could at the same time be radically simple and
    radically more expressive than all the others that had ever been written (thanks to both
    being first-class and having flavorful multiple inheritance). I liked the result so much that
    I used it in many software packages I wrote, achieving a level of simplicity and generality
    that was not available to me in Common Lisp, OCaml or Haskell (see for instance the trie
    implementation, and its merkleized extension in gerbil-persist).

    ASDF, the de facto standard build system for Common Lisp (successor to DEFSYSTEM,
    vaguely analogous to Make in C), and turned it into ASDF 2, making it vastly more
    usable: robust, portable (especially wrt pathnames), easy to configure, with support for
    caching fasls (output files) separately per implementation. A crucial technique that un-
    locked the social acceptability of new features was the ability to upgrade ASDF after
    installation: before that, users were locked with the vendor-provided version so had in-
    centive to always support the worst version of ASDF, which means vendors had no incen-
    tive to upgrade. Dynamic upgradability reversed the incentives, illustrating the feedback
    between technology and social dynamics. In general, ASDF was made to better fulfill
    its role of supporting modularity, as characterized by the subtitle: more cooperation, less
    coordination.

Douglas T. Ross.        A Generalized Technique for Symbol Manipulation and Nu-
   merical Calculation. Communications of the ACM 4(3), pp. 147–150, 1961.
   doi:10.1145/366199.366256.          Introduces Ross’s plex representation—built from
   what we would today call records, or structs—a generalized structure in memory whose
   components may contain data, links (pointers to more data), or even code to jump to (not
   just a pointer to the address to jump to, but the actual transfer instruction, which can
   itself be jumped to and will then typically transfer control to the correct fixed-address
   subroutine). One of the tricks Ross proposes and names “reversed use of index register”
   consists in having a fixed offset from an object at a variable address in the register,
   whereas the normal usage expected by everyone else was a variable offset in the register
   to an object at a fixed address. Very clever and low-level—the paper also illustrates the
   level of abstraction at which most programmers were thinking at the time, for the paper
   to even be published.
        Ross doesn’t say whether the index register is to be used as an argument by the code
   being jumped to—which would be an early example of what I’d call U-encoding. The
   indexed transfer certainly preserves the index register, and for the routine being called to
   reuse the value in that register rather than clobber it is the most natural extension of the
386                                                     ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY

      idea, without even having to conceptualize it as an argument being passed. Who today can
      guess what was obvious or needed to be explicitly conceptualized at a time when Ross’s
      paper was worth publishing? At least Sutherland 1963 will make that notion explicit.
      Presented earlier at the ACM Conference on Symbolic Manipulation, May 20–21, 1960.
Douglas T. Ross. Toward foundations for the understanding of type. In Proc. Pro-

Jerome H. Saltzer. The “Principle of Least Privilege” and Multics. Massachusetts Institute of
    Technology, Project MAC, CSR-RFC 35, 1973. https://web.mit.edu/Saltzer/ww
