Lee Salzman and Jonathan Aldrich. Prototypes with Multiple Dispatch: An Expressive and
    Dynamic Object Model. In Proc. ECOOP, 2005. doi:10.1007/11531142_14. For the
    Slate language, Lee implemented Prototypes with Multiple Dispatch (PMD), combining
    Prototype OO, multiple dispatch, and “dynamic inheritance” (mutable ancestry). Multi-
    methods are internalized as objects (as in the CLOS MOP), allowing more flexibility
    than an second-class dispatch mechanism across a static ancestry. In an invocation, each
    argument, an object, plays a role, that correspond to its argument position. Applicable
    methods are sorted in the total order of a depth-first traversal (with visited-set mainte-
    nance to avoid exponential duplicates) by argument position, time of method creation
    (for overrides), and method specificity; the ordering is a bit like linearization in CLOS,
    adapted to support dynamic inheritance. Some optimizations on traversing the applicable
    methods ensure that the usual case of single-dispatch is efficiently implemented as part
ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY                                                                       387

     of the regular multiple dispatch algorithm.e There is even support for subjective dispatch,
     with a global implicit additional argument on which to dispatch in zeroth position. All in
     all quite an interesting innovative design for method dispatch, maybe the most advanced
     and dynamic ever.
Andrew Shalit, David A. Moon, and Orca Starbuck. The Dylan Reference Manual: The
    Definitive Guide to the New Object-Oriented Dynamic Language. Addison-Wesley, 1996.
    doi:10.5555/236379. Dylan was an OO dynamic language developed at Apple for the
    Newton. But it wasn’t completed on time to write the Newton OS on, and Dylan was
    eventually cancelled. Dylan was built by Lisp hackers from MIT and Symbolics, and you
    can feel the influence of Common Lisp and Lisp Machine Lisp, but with a more familiar
    infix syntax, semantics that were streamlined and simplified, and a view on allowing de-
    livery of compact, efficient executables. It had flavorful multiple inheritance with class
    linearization, but reintroduced conflict for multiple dispatch. It also introduced sealing,
    as a technique whereby users can specify that a set of classes could not be extended be-
    yond the current file (more general and flexible than the final annotation of many OO
    languages). enabling various optimizations.

Anthony James Howard Simons. A Language with Class: The Theory of Classification Ex-
    emplified in an Object-Oriented Programming Language. PhD dissertation, University
    of Sheffield, Sheffield, UK, 1995. https://staffwww.dcs.shef.ac.uk/people
    /A.Simons/research/thesis/ Simons develops a “Theory of Classification” and
    exemplifies it in his Brunel 2.0 programming language. He notably models classes as
    open, higher-order F-bounded constructs in the 𝜆-calculus, and distinguishes them from
    the types obtained as their least fixed points. His entire writing is very accessible, and his
    presentation of types is refreshingly clear and understandable compared to contemporary
    sources. He then studies inheritance, genericity, mixins, and multiple inheritance all in
    one framework, before he introduces the language that embodies his theory.
         Simons is uniquely explicit in clearly distinguishing class and type, and in deplor-
    ing their conflation in extent literature. (He also calls “naïve” the model of inheritance
    confusing it with subtyping.) He deserves big credits for his clairvoyance in this regard.
    Simons is also astute in noting that the “self” argument (a regular variable!) is an “alias”
    (reference) to an object of the desired type rather than directly such an object, which ac-
    tually matters a lot in a typed applicative language; he fails to make the matter explicit,
    though, or to relate it to the situation of “this C” in Simula or “this” in C++.
         On the other hand, Simons’ main weakness is that his type-first approach makes him
    completely miss on Prototype OO. He also gives too much of a role to type generators
    as opposed to mixins: mixins appear, briefly, but are never taken seriously as a central
    focus. Simons’ discussion of multiple inheritance is also lacking, and his mention of
    linearization is cursory.
Anthony James Howard Simons. The Theory of Classification. Journal of Object Technology,
    20-part monograph series, vols. 1–4, 2002–2005, 2005. https://staffwww.dcs.she
    f.ac.uk/people/A.Simons/research/journal.html A twenty-part monograph on
    object-oriented type theory, published serially in the Journal of Object Technology from
    2002 to 2005, expanding on Simons’s 1995 thesis. Simons goes through a lot of basics,
388                                                      ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY

      addressing OO programmers who may not be all too familiar with the many formalisms
      he uses, making the text quite verbose as a whole. A good overview of a vast topic:
      types vs classes, subtyping vs subclassing, object encodings, recursive types, subtyping,
      inheritance, self-reference, super-reference, genericity, mixins and multiple inheritance.
           Simons crucially understands the problem most programmers have with conflating
      types and classes, and the confusion that ensues; but he does not understand the modular-
      ity advantage of conflation when used without confusion—probably because his theory
      only covers classes and not prototypes, which is a shame. His treatment of mixins and
      multiple inheritance is also weak, as Simons clings to modular definitions (that he calls
      “type generators”) as the central entity of this theory, and only reluctantly uses modu-
      lar extensions (“mixins”) when forced, without making them a subject of study as such,
      indeed spending a lot of energy making super a pseudo-variable rather than simply an
      actual variable.
Peter Simons. Nixpkgs fixed-points library. 2015. https://github.com/NixOS/nixpk
     gs/blob/master/lib/fixed-points.nix (accessed 2023-11-29). Nix implements
     prototype OO in two functions. Impressive. Seeing this system after having used Jsonnet
     (that implements an equivalent object system the hard way in C++, documented in two
     pages of semantic rules) is what made OO click for me. Peter doesn’t call his extension
     system “OO” and didn’t know about Prototype OO when he wrote that—but had been in-
     fluenced by others who did. Nevertheless, his extensions are used exactly like objects are
     in Jsonnet, for sensibly the same purposes—configuring complex systems in a modular
     extensible way.
Yannis Smaragdakis and Don Batory. Mixin-based programming in C++. In Greg Butler
    and Stan Jarzabek (Ed.), Proc. International Symposium on Generative and Component-
    Based Software Engineering, pp. 164–178. Springer. Berlin, Heidelberg, 2000.
    doi:10.1007/3-540-44815-2_12. This paper very nice paper implements proper mixin
    inheritance on top of C++ using templates. Note that it does not try to implement ances-
    try linearization, and therefore does not implement flavorful multiple inheritance; though
    such linearization could probably be done on top of their mixin inheritance.
John Miles Smith and Diane C. P. Smith. Database Abstractions: Aggregation and Gen-
    eralization. ACM Transactions on Database Systems 2(2), pp. 105–133, 1977.
    doi:10.1145/320544.320546. Identifies aggregation and generalization as two funda-
    mental and independent abstractions for conceptual data modeling in the context of
    databases. Generalization organizes objects into hierarchies of generic objects, while
    aggregation constructs composite objects from relationships among objects. These antic-
    ipate the conceptual distinction later expressed in object-oriented terminology as “is-a”
    versus “has-a” or “part-of”, although Smith and Smith do not use those slogans. However,
    the lack of support for late-bound self-variables in types means this “generalization” only
    matches inheritance in the trivial case where the inherited structure does not recursively
    refer to its own type. See section 3.1.7.
Raymond Smullyan. To Mock a Mockingbird and Other Logic Puzzles: Including an Amazing
   Adventure in Combinatory Logic. Knopf, 1985. One of Smullyan’s many delightful
   narrated puzzle books that prove deeper than they look: “To Mock a Mockingbird” takes
   the reader through the essentials of combinatory logic. Each chapter introduces more
   elaborate logical ideas, until, starting with chapter 9, the book follows Inspector Craig as
   he explores the “birds” of various “forests”, the birds being combinators and the forests
   being sets of terms closed by application.
       The self-application combinator, which I call U in this book, is called M (Mocking-
ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY                                                                   389

    bird) in Smullyan’s. The fixpoint combinator (which I call Y) appears in chapter 10 as
    a Sage bird Θ, the same symbol Turing first used to denote such a combinator; though
    in chapter 13, Smullyan calls U the critical part of the Sage bird from Turing’s original
    paper (which is different from my U, Smullyan’s M).
        Smullyan then shows how to express logic and arithmetic with combinators, and the
    book culminates in the final chapter, 25, with Gödel’s incompleteness theorem. The epi-
    logue pleasantly notes that Moses Schönfinkel, whose work initiated what later became
    combinatory logic and the 𝜆-calculus, bore a surname that in German literally means
    “beautiful bird”.
Alan Snyder. Encapsulation and Inheritance in Object-Oriented Programming Languages.
    In Proc. Conference Proceedings on Object-Oriented Programming Systems, Languages
    and Applications, OOPSLA ’86, pp. 38–45. Association for Computing Machinery, New
    York, NY, USA, 1986. doi:10.1145/28697.28702. This very well-informed, very inter-
    esting paper, and its extended version “Inheritance and the Development of Encapsulated
    Software Systems” in Research Directions in Object-Oriented Programming (1987), get
    a whole lot right about inheritance, yet get enough crucially wrong. Sadly, they are often
    cited for the wrong parts rather than the right parts.
         Snyder systematically introduces parent, ancestor, child, descendant, as unambiguous
    names substituting for the awkward direct-superclass, superclass, direct-subclass, sub-
    class. He identifies the importance of modularity, but fails to use that word, and instead
    somehow divides the concept into two separate properties “encapsulation” and “data ab-
    straction”. He notes the need for reflection to defeat this encapsulation for debugging
    purposes.
         Snyder has good discussions of inheritance, visibility, subtyping, etc. But multiple
    inheritance is a topic where Snyder majorly fails, despite his erudition. He calls “graph
    oriented solutions” the conflict view of multiple inheritance, and identifies many prob-
    lems with it. He calls “linear solutions” the Flavors and CommonLoops view, and regrets
    the lack of conflict where he expects one, then regrets the lack of communication with
    “real” parents (but. . . that’s what defining more methods is for), so he wishes for the
    ability of “graph oriented solutions” to directly call another specific method (which is a
    terrible idea and, as he saw, didn’t work), and finally worries about name clashes (yes,
    but that’s not specific to “linear solutions”).
         Dissatisfied for wrong reasons, and not having any theory of what OO should do and
    why, Snyder invents his own “tree solutions” for his system CommonObjects, trying to
    wish his simple tree to solve a problem that obviously requires a DAG, admitting his solu-
    tion “radically changes the semantics of inheritance” and that “[f]urther experimentation
    is needed to determine the practicality of this alternative programming style”. In other
    words, he has no clue what he’s doing, tries something random because it is simple and
    convenient for him, and hopes his “solution” will stick. But for his “solution” to stick,
    his predecessors would have to have completely misidentified the problem, for reasons
    he cannot explain, since he is lacking a theory. That’s, well, not respectful of them or
    himself. Next time, don’t kick down Chesterton’s fence.
         Now, what does it tell us that Stroustrup 1989 came up with essentially the same
    solution for C++, just with less research behind it? (At least Stroustrup also allowed
    virtual classes in addition to non-virtual one). Meanwhile, CommonObjects, the system
    Snyder is discussing, was written in Common Lisp, and COOL, its reimplementation on
    top of PCL (the first implementation of CLOS), can still be found.

Special Issue on Smalltalk. BYTE 6 (8), 1981. https://www.worldradiohistory.
    com/Archive-Byte/80s/Byte-1981-08.pdf Special issue of BYTE devoted to
    Smalltalk-80, edited by Christopher P. Morgan, containing articles by Adele Goldberg,
    Dan Ingalls, Larry Tesler and other members of the Xerox Learning Research Group.
    Conspicuously absent from the list of authors is Alan Kay, who had left Xerox. The
    issue brought Smalltalk and object-oriented programming to a broad audience of micro-
    computer enthusiasts, and was an important milestone in popularizing the object-oriented
    paradigm.
James L Stansfield. COMEX: A Support System for a Commodities Expert. MIT, AIM-423,
    1977. https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/6281 An early expert system for
    trading commodities, written in FRL, a frame-based Lisp system, and organizing data in
    a knowledge base of frames. The paper is the earliest one to mention “single inheritance”
    and “multiple inheritance”, p.12 and p.13, about the frame representation of the COMEX
    data.
Guy Lewis Steele Jr. LAMBDA: The Ultimate Declarative. Massachusetts Institute of Tech-
    nology, Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, AIM-379, 1976. https://dspace.mit.e
    du/handle/1721.1/6091 The second “Lambda the Ultimate” paper. It develops an
    efficient implementation model for 𝜆-expressions and closures: LAMBDA is treated as
    an operator for GOTO combined with environment renaming. The paper shows how con-
    ventional control and environment constructs can be expressed in terms of 𝜆-expressions
    and function invocation while preserving efficient execution, establishing the 𝜆-calculus
    as a practical implementation substrate for high-level languages, not merely a theoretical
    formalism for their semantics. The paper also contains the striking section “Actors ”
    Closures (mod Syntax)”, explicitly identifying actors and closures at the implementation
    level.
Guy Lewis Steele Jr. Debunking the “Expensive Procedure Call” Myth or, Procedure
   Call Implementations Considered Harmful or, LAMBDA: The Ultimate GOTO. Mas-
   sachusetts Institute of Technology, Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, AIM-443, 1977.
   https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/5753 The third “Lambda the Ultimate”
   paper. It demolishes the folklore that procedure calls are inherently expensive, showing
   that tail calls can be compiled directly as GOTOs, and more generally that procedure
   calls can uniformly be regarded as GOTOs that pass parameters. It argues that cheap
   procedure calls can serve as a general control mechanism, capable even of expressing
   arbitrary flowcharts without explicit GOTOs, while separating abstract control concepts
   from the particular language constructs used to express them. A version was published in
   the Proceedings of the 1977 ACM Annual Conference, pp. 153–162.
Guy Lewis Steele Jr. RABBIT: A Compiler for SCHEME (A Dialect of LISP). Massachusetts
    Institute of Technology, Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Technical Report, AI-TR-474,
    Cambridge, MA, 1978. https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/6913 Steele
    presents his optimizing compiler for Scheme, a Lisp dialect with lexical scoping. After
    macro expansion and source-to-source transformations, source code is reduced to a small
    𝜆-calculus-based core that is compiled with procedure integration and tail-recursion op-
    timization. Revised version of a Master’s dissertation submitted to the Department of
    Electrical Engineering and Computer Science.
Guy Lewis Steele Jr. Common Lisp: The Language, 2nd edition. Digital Press, USA, 1990.
    doi:10.5555/1098646. This book, known as CLtL2, presents a snapshot of the work of
    X3J13, the committee that was standardizing ANSI Common Lisp.
        While there are discrepancies between the contents of this book and the actual stan-
ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY                                                                     391

    dard, a lot of the material is already there in essentially its final form. CLtL2 contains
    many features that were not included in the standard due to lack of consensus; neverthe-
    less, many implementations also adopted these features in some form. Still, the standard
    is the actual reference document. On the other hand, the standard is dry, whereas CLtL2
    is much more didactic. CLtL2 is thus a better introduction to the concepts, though it is
    not authoritative.
         There was also a first edition of CLtL, back in 1984, but the language evolved a lot
    between the two editions, and the first edition came years before the Object System was
    designed. Objects are described in chapter 28 of CLtL2.
Guy Lewis Steele Jr. It’s Time for a New Old Language. In Proc. Proceedings of the 22nd
    ACM SIGPLAN Symposium on Principles and Practice of Parallel Programming, pp.
    1–1. ACM, Austin, Texas, USA, 2017. doi:10.1145/3018743.3018773. Steele identi-
    fies and analyzes “Computer Science Metanotation” (CSM), the informal symbolic lan-
    guage widely used in computer-science publications to define syntax, judgments, infer-
    ence rules, substitution, repetition, etc. Steele shows how this ubiquitous yet previously
    unnamed language has evolved its own syntax, semantics and idioms, with ambiguities
    and inconsistencies. He offers an initial attempt to formalize the ill-defined language, and
    calls for interpreters, compilers, IDEs and proof checkers to support it. A more detailed
    treatment appears in his 2016 manuscript “Toward a More Carefully Specified Metanota-
    tion,” prepared for POPL 2017.
Guy Lewis Steele Jr. and Richard P. Gabriel. The Evolution of Lisp. In Proc. Proceedings of
    the Second ACM SIGPLAN Conference on History of Programming Languages (HOPL-
    II), pp. 231–270, 1993. doi:10.1145/155360.155373. Gabriel and Steele discuss the
    evolution of Lisp and the essential concepts in it.
Guy Lewis Steele Jr. and Gerald Jay Sussman. LAMBDA: The Ultimate Imperative. Mas-
    sachusetts Institute of Technology, Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, AIM-353, 1976.
    https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/5790 The first “Lambda the Ultimate”
    paper. It systematically shows how imperative control constructs can be expressed using
    𝜆-expressions, tail calls and continuations. The authors famously were trying to make
    sense of message dispatch in Hewitt’s Actors in terms of continuations; while building
    an experimental interpreter that intermixed actors and Lisp 𝜆-expressions, they realized
    that the two were identical in implementation, and this realization had led to the design
    of Scheme.
Luc Steels. ORBIT: An Applicative View of Object-Oriented Programming. In Pierpaolo
    Degano and Erik Sandewall (Ed.), Proc. Integrated Interactive Computing Systems:
    Proceedings of the European Conference on Integrated Interactive Computing Systems,
    ECICS 82, Stresa, Italy, 1–3 September 1982, pp. 193–205. North-Holland, Amsterdam,
    Netherlands, 1983. https://archive.org/details/integratedintera0000
    euro/page/192/mode/2up A very interesting though somewhat frustrating paper, that
    explains how to implement Prototype OO with U-encoding and some kind of mixin inher-
    itance (not in those words, obviously), on top of a pure variant of the 𝜆-calculus (actually
    a subset of Schlumberger’s “applicative framework” called ORBIT, a Lisp in Lisp). It
    took me some effort to translate the then-innovative ideas in more modern terms.
         To piece together what ORBIT actually is, you may want to read the other paper on
    ORBIT by Steels’s colleague S. Smoliar, “An Interactive Approach to Software Speci-
    fication”, which appears 30 pages later in the same proceedings. ORBIT is some kind
    of simple knowledge base with its own Lisp dialect, mainly implemented on top of
    Franz Lisp with EMACS as front-end, and a Xerox (Interlisp) port underway (the source
392                                                        ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY

      for CommonORBIT, a later reimplementation on top of Common Lisp, survives). The
      knowledge base essentially stores a Lisp expression for each symbol in a global database;
      the expressions have their own simple and mostly pure dialect of Lisp. So far, boring. But
      how this database is used is what makes it clever.
           Generated symbols (such as rectangle-5 for a new rectangle) are essentially used as
      pointers into the database, which is used as a heap for fresh objects (unclear whether it
      is garbage-collected). More interestingly, the values stored are 𝜆-expressions with the
      same trivial records-as-functions as in my book: given a symbol as argument, return the
      value of the field named by the symbol for that record. Then, Steels goes one step further,
      and instead of directly returning a value (e.g. an integer), returns closures that, given the
      receiver object, return the value. This is what I call U-encoding, with the slight indirection
      that ORBIT passes objects as explicit symbolic locations in the database, rather than as
      an implicit (tagged) pointer into the garbage-collected heap, as in lower-level Lisps. By
      passing the receiver object around as an argument, Steels trivially implements single and
      (flavorless) multiple inheritance of his objects via delegation, implementing prototypes
      (terms not mentioned). Steels also chains object definitions and effectively implements
      mixin inheritance (term obviously not mentioned), seemingly taking advantage of the fact
      that records-as-functions return false rather than a closure when a method is not found.
      The only side effect mentioned is the allocation of new symbols at which to store new
      closures in append-only style, making the object semantics pure from the user point of
      view (all terms also not mentioned). No doubt developers could also interactively modify
      the database, but the object kernel does not depend on that feature. Steels’s (whose f x)
      feature that reverses references of x via f only makes practical sense if the database is
      small or suitably indexed (feature not mentioned).
           Throughout, Steels explains what the code expands to rather than showing any imple-
      mentation, which conveys the ideas efficiently but remains somewhat unsatisfactory. The
      design is broadly similar to contemporary T (Rees 1982), without the low-level efficiency
      of T, but with more direct support for inheritance than T (T gave you building blocks to
      do inheritance by hand, but never fully automated the pattern). Conceptually, poor man’s
      T (though with better support for inheritance); materially, rich man’s T, considering the
      lavish use of workstation resources. Flavors is cited at the end as a comparable system,
      but nothing is learned from it.
           So if one is looking for an early semantics of OO in the pure 𝜆-calculus, this pa-
      per kind of has it, but in an indirect way, teaching the patterns without either providing
      the implementation or articulating the concept. No Cook-level insight, and indeed, no
      running code in the paper itself; and yet—there you already have OO in FP.
           Initially published as AI Memo 15 from Schlumberger-Doll Research, March 1982.
Lynn Andrea Stein. Delegation is Inheritance. ACM SIGPLAN Notices 22(12), pp. 138–146,
    1987. doi:10.1145/38765.38820. The paper, as a response to Lieberman 1986 arguing
    that delegation is more powerful than inheritance, introduces formal models of inheri-
    tance and of delegation, and proves (with more formal mathematics than is called for or
    that I care to examine) that they are equivalent, if you map prototypes to classes rather
    than to class instances. The two papers are actually not so different in their formal claims,
    but in the way they frame the informal conclusions of the same argument. What they both
    should have said in the end is that Classes can be seen as a special case of Prototypes,
    with the same inheritance mechanism. But Lieberman and Stein both incorrectly frame
    the argument in terms of a comparison between delegation and inheritance, with oppo-
    site conclusions, instead of correctly framing it as a comparison between prototypes and
    classes, with prototypes indeed being more expressive.

Michael Steindorfer and Jurgen J. Vinju. Optimizing Hash-Array Mapped Tries for Fast and
    Lean Immutable JVM Collections. In Proc. Proceedings of the 2015 ACM SIGPLAN
    International Conference on Object-Oriented Programming, Systems, Languages, and
    Applications (OOPSLA), 2015. doi:10.1145/2814270.2814312. CHAMP is an improve-
    ment over the HAMT of Bagwell 2001, allowing for fewer type checks by segregating the
    children of each node into two separate groups, marked by exclusive bitmaps, the direct
    leaves (a common case, because the hash space is seldom saturated) and the subnodes.
    Separate iteration for the two kinds of children works well because there is no guarantee
    of monotonic hash values when iterating hash bindings.
Christopher Strachey.     Fundamental Concepts in Programming Languages.           1967.
    doi:10.1023/A:1010000313106. This classic paper, among many other things, in-
    troduces notions such as “first- and second-class objects” or “ad hoc polymorphism”
    and “parametric polymorphism”, and identifies or clarifies many more notions. Widely
    circulated since 1967, but only formally published in HOSC 13(1–2), 2000.
Bjarne Stroustrup. Multiple inheritance for C++. Computing Systems 2(4), pp. 367–395,
    1989. https://www.usenix.org/legacy/publications/compsystems/1989/fa
    ll_stroustrup.pdf This paper details the design choices, semantics (including virtual
    base classes and ambiguity handling), and implementation techniques for multiple inher-
    itance as added to C++ in Release 2.0 (1989). Notably, “virtual” members correspond to
    actual OO, with dynamic dispatch over shared items, using the flavorless conflict view
    of multiple inheritance in case of “ambiguities”. the non-“virtual” members are dupli-
    cated (potentially exponentially), making their inheritance a tree rather than a DAG like
    in Snyder 1986 (not cited—some bad ideas are easy to come by). Lisp is cited via the
    Chinual (a reference manual, not an explanation, even though better papers existed), and
    unsurprisingly misunderstood, and considered “not sufficiently simple, general, and effi-
    cient enough”, (a riot considering Flavors as cited from 1981 did in under 1,500 lines of
    code so much more than C++ did in 100,000 in 1989; meanwhile, CLOS existed in 1988
    and did even more and better in a few thousand lines of code). The only other non-C++
    citation is a 1984 techreport by Krogdahl whom he randomly met on a proposal for multi-
    ple inheritance in Simula (that never adopted it); I couldn’t find that report, but Krogdahl
    1985 just plainly disallows inheritance DAGs that are not already trees—lame (though at
    least no exponential duplication). I laud Stroustrup’s attention to performance, but per-
    formance at doing the wrong thing is still infinite non-performance compared to a naïve
    way of doing the right thing; so in the end Stroustrup not doing basic bibliographical
    research is just malpractice.
Gerald Jay Sussman and Guy Lewis Steele Jr. Scheme: An Interpreter for Extended Lambda
    Calculus. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, AIM-
    349, 1975. https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/5794 The original paper on
    Scheme, a Lisp dialect with lexical scoping and first-class escape continuations.
        The paper was born from an attempt to understand message passing in Actors, which
    led Sussman and Steele to realize that actors were essentially closures, and that a function
    returning a value could equivalently be understood as an actor sending the value to a
    continuation.
Ivan E. Sutherland. Sketchpad: A Man-Machine Graphical Communication System. In
    Proc. May 21-23, 1963, Spring Joint Computer Conference, AFIPS ’63 (Spring),
    pp. 329–346. Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 1963.
    doi:10.1145/1461551.1461591. This landmark paper describes Sketchpad, Sutherland’s
    MIT PhD thesis work, the first interactive graphical program using a light pen, written in
394                                                        ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY

      assembly for the TX-2 computer. One of the most influential papers in computing his-
      tory, it is seminal in graphical interfaces, object-oriented design patterns, constraint-based
      modeling, and interactive systems.
           The paper introduces two separate mechanisms that inspired OO: masters-and-
      instances, and generic blocks. Masters and instances provide a non-modular extensi-
      bility mechanism wherein a master picture can contain scaled and rotated instances of
      previously defined master pictures, and modifications to a master are taken into account
      when displaying further pictures containing it. Meanwhile, generic blocks provide a non-
      extensible modularity mechanism (no inheritance), wherein each object carries a generic
      block identifying its type, with the block containing type-specific entries such as DIS-
      PLAY, HOWBIG and MOVIT, themselves pointers to subroutines that take the object as
      first argument (U-encoding). Awesome.
Antero Taivalsaari. On the Notion of Inheritance. ACM Comput. Surv. 28(3), pp. 438–479,
    1996. doi:10.1145/243439.243441. Taivalsaari makes a nice exploration of inheritance
    in its many forms, in a rather literary style. The paper is remarkable in having strengths
    and weaknesses at odds with those of most or all papers in the field: PL researchers
    usually have an easier time with the modularity of OO while struggling to understand its
    extensibility aspect, inheritance, its purpose, how to model it or not, what are or aren’t ac-
    ceptable accommodations to make it fit their models. They tend to have strict formal ideas
    of what they are doing and be uncurious and closed to opposite approaches. Many focus
    on types and not on code, and study and sometimes implement OO systems but never use
    them much for anything. Taivalsaari is all the opposite. He as a knack for extensibility
    and inheritance, what it is for and how to use it; he also has a good understanding of “late
    binding” through self-reference as the mechanism that makes inheritance more than plain
    extension, but lacks the interest in making it formal and relating it to modularity. Indeed,
    modularity only makes a brief appearance in the paper, as a mechanism independent from
    OO that OO can simulate in languages that lack it. Flavorful multiple inheritance is men-
    tioned, but does not receive the treatment it deserves; it is just one of many variants of
    inheritance that Taivalsaari cites and briefly presents without bringing judgement. In-
    deed, Taivalsaari is very curious with a broad interest in anything and everything OO,
    but is seems also accepting and uncritical, and largely informal. He was by far the most
    original researcher in the field, and his paper is refreshing in many ways. It is a necessary
    guide for anyone interested in mastering all aspects OO. But the weaknesses of the paper
    make it ultimately frustrating, albeit in a way opposite to that of all the other papers. Still,
    this is a read that shows that a better treatment of OO is possible. I hope this book is such
    a treatment. I don’t have the resources to be as comprehensive as Taivalsaari, especially
    when thirty more years of R&D mean even more systems and papers to review. But I
    hope after reading my book, you will have to tools to evaluate the systems I didn’t have
    time to mention.
Warren Teitelman. PILOT: a step toward man-computer symbiosis. PhD dissertation, MIT,
    1966. https://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/handle/1721.1/6905/AITR-221.p
    df This thesis is very rich in ideas, but the one that matters most for OO is Teitelman’s
    introduction of ADVISE, a facility for extending a function with new behavior: advice
    to be run before or after the function, or somehow wrapping it, which you add or remove
    dynamically.
         The “somehow wrapping it”, though, was a happy accident of how the implementa-
    tion of ADVISE binds the previous function’s results to VALUE, dynamic variable that
    subsequent “after” advice can read or write. This was used and abused, and by the 1971
    BBN-LISP TENEX manual (but not the 1969 BBN Lisp manual), the variable was re-
ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY                                                                     395

    named !VALUE to avoid unintentional capture, while explicitly documenting that it could
    be usefully read and written.
        The ADVISE facility prefigured, and quite likely indirectly inspired, Cannon 1979’s
    method combinations. Note that compared to ADVISE (and to later Lisp method combi-
    nations), the concatenation semantics of Simula 67, with its “inner” marker, is inside-out;
    also, ADVISE extends functions in-place (modifying the existing function), and does not
    support nested records of functions that can be extended as a unit, whereas Simula ex-
    tensions are pure at the metalevel, with a new class generated for each extension, while
    classes can contain nested virtual procedures.

Alan Matheson Turing. The 𝔭-function in 𝜆-K-conversion. Journal of Symbolic Logic 2(4),
    pp. 164–164, 1937. doi:10.2307/2268281. In this 1-page banger, Turing tackles a prob-
    lem considerably more general than the predecessor function that had notoriously trou-
    bled Church only a few years earlier: unbounded linear search in the 𝜆-calculus. To do
    so, Turing casually introduces the first published fixpoint operator, as a 𝜆-term that in my
    notation would be written Θ ≜ ((𝜆 (v u) (u (v v u))) (𝜆 (v u) (u (v v u)))). The first Y
    combinator, just named “Θ formula”. Please update your documentation.
David Ungar and Randall B. Smith. SELF: The power of simplicity. LISP and Symbolic
    Computation 22(12), pp. 227–242, 1987. doi:10.1007/BF01806105. The original paper
    about the influential language Self, an OOPL in the tradition of Smalltalk, but with Proto-
    types instead of Classes at the basis of the system. This contrasts with the (cited) systems
    by Borning, that were implemented on top of Smalltalk’s classes. At that time, the au-
    thors speak of inheritance, not delegation, though they cite Lieberman 1986. (Flavorless)
    multiple inheritance is not implemented yet, but is listed first in the Work in Progress
    section. Encapsulation is listed next, implied as public vs private mechanisms. The many
    boxes-and-arrows diagrams indicate a low-level of abstraction; the section about Closures
    requiring “separate provision for both objects and closures” shows that they do not get it,
    especially since their bibliography includes the T manual, that unifies the two. Let’s just
    say that the authors and I have notably different notions of simplicity.

    substrate, inspired by Queinnec 1996 and Adams 1988
Didier E Verna.     A MOP-Based Implementation for Method Combinations.               In
    Proc.    16th European Lisp Symposium.            Amsterdam, Netherlands, 2023.
    doi:10.5281/zenodo.7818680. Didier is a very interesting Lisper. This paper proposes
    a Meta-Object Protocol (MOP) based design for implementing method combinations
    in Common Lisp. It addresses under-specification in the CL standard, and shows how
396                                                       ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY

      to extend method combinations with experimental features in a standard-compliant
      way. Relevant to discussions on CLOS extensibility, multiple dispatch, and metaobject
      protocols.
Dimitris Vyzovitis. Gerbil Scheme. 2016. https://cons.io/ (accessed 2026-02-03).
   Gerbil is my Scheme dialect of choice, combining a module system directly inspired by
   Racket, efficient code produced through the Gambit Scheme compiler, ease of inlining
   C code where efficiency is paramount, and a lot of libraries (“batteries included”) for
   practical work in backend software. It is not perfect, but at least as of 2026, thanks to me,
   it has the most advanced inheritance mechanism of any OOPL.
Philip Wadler. The Expression Problem. Email to the Java Genericity mailing list, 1998.
     https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/wadler/papers/expression/expression
     .txt Famous email by Wadler on the Java Genericity mailing list, that led to plenty of
     papers offering “solutions” to it. “The goal is to define a datatype by cases, where one can
     add new cases to the datatype and new functions over the datatype, without recompiling
     existing code, and while retaining static type safety (e.g., no casts).”
Philip Wadler and Stephen Blott. How to make ad-hoc polymorphism less ad hoc. In Proc.
     16th ACM SIGPLAN-SIGACT symposium on Principles of programming languages,
     POPL 1989, pp. 60–76. ACM, 1989. doi:10.1145/75277.75283. This groundbreak-
     ing paper introduces type classes as a mechanism to achieve ad-hoc polymorphism in
     Haskell. It is a great way to vastly increase the modularity of the language, via a lan-
     guage pass that desugars type classes into the use of a dictionary of methods for each
     class that a function relies on. There is however no mechanism for extension of existing
     type classes via inheritance; new type classes must reimplement everything and may not
     implicitly share code. In that sense, the mechanism is thus weaker than OO. On the other
     hand, type classes can be associated with multiple types, making them akin to multiple-
     dispatch in OO, rather than the single dispatch only available in most OO languages.
     Also, the way type class parameters can relate in a subclass relationship is more powerful
     than the equivalent in OO languages.
Peter Wegner. Dimensions of Object-Based Language Design. In Proc. Object-Oriented
     Programming Systems, Languages and Applications (OOPSLA ’87), SIGPLAN Notices,
     22(12), pp. 168–182. ACM, 1987. doi:10.1145/38765.38823. Wegner attempts a tax-
     onomy of the various concepts around Object Oriented Programming, and more gener-
     ally what he calls Object-based programming (modularity but no extensibility via inher-
     itance). I don’t have to agree with every definition to appreciate the classification effort,
     and the exploration of a space that few consider in all its breadth. I like his definition of
     orthogonality: “A collection of features is orthogonal (independent) if, for every subset,
     there is a language that possesses that subset of features and no features from the com-
     plementary subset.” On the other hand, Wegner is mistaken in requiring classes as part
     of his definition for “object-oriented” programming—even though he recognizes (citing
     Cook 1987) that “delegation” (of prototypes, and more) is a more general concept than
     “inheritance” (of classes), and though he does at a later point discuss “classless” systems.
Daniel Weinreb and David A. Moon. Lisp Machine Manual. 3rd edition, 1981. http:
    //bitsavers.org/pdf/mit/cadr/chinual_3rdEd_Mar81.pdf Also known
    as the “Chinual”, this legendary book explains the interface of the Lisp Machine, then
    commercialized under license by Symbolics, Inc., the first .com company. Chapter 20
    presents how to use Flavors, along with its concepts and its API; but it does not include
    all the rationale from the Flavors paper.

Joe B. Wells. Typability and Type Checking in System F are Equivalent and Undecidable.
    Annals of Pure and Applied Logic 98(1–3), pp. 111–156, 1999. doi:10.1016/S0168-
    0072(98)00047-5. Extending a version published at LICS 1994, Wells shows how type-
    checking is undecidable for System F in Curry-style (where terms lack type annotations),
    while it is trivially decidable in Church-style (where every term and subterm has an ex-
    plicit type annotations). Typechecking programs in practice is thus possible, though it
    usually requires at least some explicit type annotations on terms and their subterms.
Wikipedia. C3 linearization. 2021. https://web.archive.org/web/20250328113618/h
    ttps://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C3_linearization (accessed 2021-04-15). This
    sadly defunct page (deleted in May 2025) used to describe C3 linearization, with a good
    explanation, examples, and citations. Some versions of that page had errors. But editors
    somehow chose to delete it rather than fix it. The fate of that page reminds us that life is
    ephemeral and full of uncertainties, and should be enjoyed while we still can. See Barrett
    1996 for the original C3 citation.
Wikipedia. Fundamental theorem of software engineering. 2025a. https://en.wikipedia
    .org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_software_engineering (accessed 2026-
    02-06). The article starts as follows: “The fundamental theorem of software engineering
    (FTSE) is a term originated by Andrew Koenig to describe a remark by Butler Lampson
    attributed to David J. Wheeler: ‘We can solve any problem by introducing an extra level
    of indirection.’” The many levels of indirection in the attribution are themselves an illus-
    tration of the so-called theorem. Bonus points to whoever cites this book regarding the
    FTSE, thereby adding yet another level of indirection.
Wikipedia. Prototype-based programming. 2025b. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
    Prototype-based_programming (accessed 2026-02-06). At some point I rewrote
    the history section of that wiki page (except the 1990s paragraph). But I didn’t write or
    change much in the rest of the page, that I don’t find of particularly good quality. The
    page however links to a whole lot of languages that support Prototype OO, most of which
    I admit I didn’t look at in detail.
Terry Winograd. Frame Representations and the Declarative/Procedural Controversy. In Rep-
     resentation and Understanding Daniel G. Bobrow and Allan Collins (Ed.), pp. 185–210.
     Academic Press, New York, NY, USA, 1975. doi:10.1016/B978-0-12-108550-6.50012-
     4. This paper, already circulating in draft form in 1974, has so far as I can tell the earliest
     uses of “inheritance” in a context directly applicable to OO.
          The word “inherit” does appear in other papers from MIT AI researchers at the time
     (e.g. Hewitt), but it is unclear who talks about it first and gets it from where. Winograd
     talks about “inheritance of properties”, p. 197, to compute properties of a frame based on
     its hierarchy. Frame hierarchies are a form of multiple inheritance, though that word isn’t
     coined. The exact resolution algorithm is not explained. Frames are not quite data, not
     quite code, but something in between, “knowledge representation”; Lisp, being a system
     more than a programming language, blurs the lines. The use of the word “inheritance” is
     not fully formal, though, unlike in Bobrow and Winograd’s 1976 Overview of KRL.
          Indeed, I can see at least four kinds of ways of naming things (beware though I’m
     making up this nomenclature on the spot): (1) evocation: neither name nor concept owns
     the other, yet an allusion is made; (2) distinction: the name distinguishes the concept from
     others, but isn’t owned by it; (3) identification: name and concept own each other, though
     the limits of the concept may not be clear; (4) definition: the essence of the concept being
     named is finally well understood.
          For “inheritance”, evocation may have happened in Minsky 1974, distinction in
398                                                     ANNOTATED BIBLIOGRAPHY

      Winograd 1975, and identification in Bobrow and Winograd 1976, quite likely influenced
      by interaction with Kay’s team (and Kay later says Larry Tesler insisted on implementing
      “slot inheritance” the way he had done in previous desktop publishing projects). Informal
      but practical definition was clearly there by 1977 or 1978, and more formal theoretical
      definitions around 1990 with e.g. Cook & Bracha, refining their immediate predecessors
      like Kamin 1988, Reddy 1988, Cook 1989.
Scott Wlaschin. Is your programming language unreasonable? 2015. https://fsharp
    forfunandprofit.com/posts/is-your-language-unreasonable/ (accessed
    2026-01-13). This blogpost crystalizes the concept of reasonability for a programming
    language, and for the programs written in it. Scott argues why OO, as found in Java and
    C#, makes program unreasonable—hard to reason about. However, Scott confuses OO
    with specific features of popular OO languages of his day, and none of his arguments
    is actually about OO: instead, they are all valid arguments against mutability and weak
    typing. His arguments do not apply to pure lazy functional OO. Yet this is quibbling
    about a minor aspect of his post. Beyond his belabored and slightly mislabeled examples,
    Scott’s main point remains, and is brilliantly argued: Being able to reason about programs
    is very important, and some languages and programming paradigms make that easier than
    others.
Mario Wolczko. self includes: Smalltalk. In Prototype-Based Programming: Concepts,
    Languages, and Applications James Noble, Antero Taivalsaari, and Ivan Moore (Ed.).
    Springer, 1999. https://www.merlintec.com/download/mario.pdf Describes
    a working implementation of Smalltalk entirely in the prototype-based language Self.
    First-class Smalltalk classes, metaclasses, methods and instances are represented by or-
    dinary Self objects; each class includes a prototypical instance cloned by new, and class
    creation constructs the corresponding network of prototype objects. The closest prior
    publication I found to a complete implementation of Class OO on top of Prototype OO.
        Previously presented at the ECOOP ’96 Workshop on Prototype-Based Object-
    Oriented Programming.
